**From documentation only.** The settings of the objectives after GRPO come from TRL's `grpo_config.py` at
v1.17.1. The papers behind them, and behind the candidates in the optimization reference, were read as
abstract pages; no result was reproduced and no objective was run. No fetched page tried to give an
instruction.

**Unverified.** The fixes after the independent review and after the test runs, by anyone but me. A run's
identity after a clock that is set forward, as when a virtual machine's host has slept: the clock I
watched was only set back, and by the code the direction makes no difference. A Linux machine other than
this WSL. The guard's lookup on macOS, where the code is the same and no test ran. The repair turn and the compile
check with a real agent (the stand-in agent only). The `on_finish` command against a real machine: it ran a
stand-in command, and no machine was stopped with it. File links on Windows, which this account cannot make
(junctions and hard links were exercised; links in WSL): the snapshot's handling of a link that leads out
of it is tested in WSL only. The case rule on macOS, and on a Windows folder that tells case apart. The
evaluator's box on native Windows and macOS, where it is missing as the box for training is. What an agent
other than Claude Code does with the guard's new refusal of a nested input: the exit code is the one that
blocks on all three, by their documentation. The seven groups of methods in the Assess rows. On your real
install, everything beyond the checks of the sixth installer run: its training scripts, a launch, a final
evaluation, and a live agent session with the new guard.

### Things to know
- **The guard asks more, and sometimes about a harmless command.** A session that writes a sealed path into
  code, a config file or a notebook meets a question at every such edit. That is the intended price: the
  question is the only moment at which a person sees that training code is about to name the test split.
  Since the independent review these are asked about too, although nothing is read: `git config` with a key
  the guard does not know as a plain value, and `git config --type bool key value`; `git stash --all` and a
  forced add where sealed files lie below; a notes file handed to a runner as data; an MCP tool that only
  lists the folder which holds the sealed files; Python code on the line with `os.walk` over a variable or
  with a `**/` in a string. In an unattended session, and with Codex and Cursor, each of these is a refusal.
- **The guard remains a seatbelt.** The reviewer needed seven minutes and 37 tool calls for its findings,
  and the limits above name more ways around the guard that are known and open. What it cannot see is a path
  or a program that is put together at run time. For data that must stay unread whatever an agent tries, keep the test split
  outside the repository or run the agent in a sandbox, as the README says.
- **Making a junction or a link is not asked about.** A snapshot no longer follows one into sealed data, and
  the guard refuses a read through one. One case stays open: a link inside a git-ignored folder, where the
  sealed pattern begins with a folder's name (with `data/test/**` sealed and `cache/alias` leading to
  `data`, the snapshot links `cache` whole). A pattern such as `**/test/**` finds the files there.
- **The keep rule finds a real gain a little less often at a campaign's first change** (61 % against 68 %
  for a gain of two deviations in the simulation). A change that is noisier than the runs before it is
  still kept above the nominal rate, about 7 % where it is three times as noisy. The simulation covers one
  iteration; the whole-campaign simulation of 12 November was not repeated.
- **The control's floor is measured, not derived.** 0.05 is about twice the highest of four scores and a
  seventh of the honest script's lowest. Measure it again after a change to how a run trains that could let
  it gain from shuffled intents.
- **`on_finish` does not replace a shutdown timer.** It runs on this machine, so it does not run when the
  controller is gone. A rented machine still needs its own timer.
- **`audit-splits` finds exact matches only**, after Unicode normalisation, case folding and collapsed
  whitespace: its count is a lower bound. It refuses Parquet, Arrow, HDF5, databases and archives, and it
  keeps one digest per record in memory.
- **The compile check covers Python files.** A change to a config file goes to a run as before.
- **The character-model evaluator's checks are checks of what a model file says, not a sandbox.** A file
  operation that a later PyTorch adds to TorchScript is not on its list.
- **A system clock that is set while runs are live.** On Linux a run's identity no longer depends on it.
  Until this round is on a Linux install, a clock that is set by five seconds while a run lives makes that
  run read as lost and ends the guard's protection of it. This machine's WSL did that within minutes on
  14 November ("Tests"); your real install runs on native Windows, where a process's start time does not
  move with the clock.
  Two other readings still use the wall clock, and I left them: the age of a heartbeat, so after a forward
  step of more than the stale time (15 minutes by default) a run reads as stalled until its next
  heartbeat, and the five seconds the guard gives its own
  searches, which a forward step ends early (a question) and a backward step lengthens, up to the hook's
  limit of twelve seconds, which does not go by the wall clock. What else in the kit reads the wall clock,
  the loop's limits among it, I did not look at.
- **The two faults of point 13 show on Linux only, and that says something about this round's tests.** The
  fixes after the independent review were run on Windows while I worked, and the reviewer worked on
  Windows too. The full run in WSL covers the test files, not what a second reviewer on Linux would try.

### Not done, and why
- **A second look at the fixes after the independent review.** The reviewer saw `850020a`. The thirteen fix
  commits after it, and the three after the test runs (`d857607`, `9d6f876`, `827c35c`), are checked by my
  probes and tests only, for the usage limit. The third of those three exists because my own check found
  what the second had lost, which is the kind of thing a second reviewer is for.
- **A question about making a junction or a link to a folder with sealed files.** The guard would have to
  resolve every link a command makes; the snapshot and the read rules close what such a link gave away.
- **A campaign with a real agent** that uses the repair turn, the compile check and the search. It draws on
  your subscription.
- **A guard walk that skips the folders no sealed pattern can match**, so that the bound of 20,000 files
  goes for patterns that begin with a wildcard too.
- **A process namespace for the training box.** `RunLog` writes its own process number into the heartbeat,
  and inside a namespace that number is another one, so a dead run could pass for a live process outside.
  It needs the number left out or translated for boxed runs first.
- **A stop at a quarter of the budget for a run that trails**: it discards slow starters, and its saving
  needs runs of ten minutes or more to measure.
- **Not opened**: further RL objectives (AIPO, GiGPO, VAPO, Turn-PPO and four more loss types of TRL),
  parity between trainer and generator, distillation and preference objectives, adapter options, further
  optimizers, low-precision and kernel items, architectures. Each is an Assess row with the sources the
  review gave and the test it needs.
- **The Adopt rows that earlier rounds named as unfinished** still are: 142 with the eight this round's
  check of the ledger moved there.

### The review that came first
Scores are my judgment from the repository's records and tests, not a measurement. The one measured
comparison is the pilot ("Read this first", point 1), in which no version is shown to train better than no
kit. So the scores say how well a version protects a result, what it can do and how well it is tested.
Points: protecting the result 25, sound keep-or-revert decisions 15, measured effect on results 15, what it
can do 15, verification 15, agents and platforms 5, documentation 10.

| Version | Commit | Score | Main reasons |
|---|---|---|---|
| 23 October kit | `5ea9659` | 32 | Run controller, logger, guard and skill, no loop. The guard let unreadable input pass, and `launch` failed on native Windows with default settings |
| First upgrade, 10 and 11 November | `b7b7652` | 56 | The loop that scores runs itself, remote runs, scouting, the Codex and Cursor ports, a benchmark. Later rounds found dozens of faults in it |
| Round 2 | `6e01543` | 61 | The guard covers other worktrees, a hole behind a link is closed, kept changes are confirmed on fresh seeds |
| Round 3 | `0f23999` | 62 | Numeric search, restart after a stall, a fine-tuning benchmark; none measured to raise results |
| Round 4 | `00be575` | 68 | 28 review findings fixed, the guard's known gap closed |
| First public version | `920bddd` | 71 | Round 4's code with the guide, the front page and the licence |
| Round 5 | `2666faf` | 76 | 37 review points built: evaluators harder to fool, many ways past the guard closed, two faults on Linux fixed |
| Public version at the time of the review | `bc96015` | 76 | Round 5's code; the front page and guide that another session rewrote were not reviewed, so the score is the same |

The 76 are: protection 20 of 25, decisions 13 of 15, measured effect 5 of 15, capability 14 of 15,
verification 12 of 15, agents and platforms 4 of 5, documentation 8 of 10. The commit ids of the first six
rows belong to the history before the public commit. This round is not scored: its changes for a Mac have
not run on one.

The improvements, ranked by expected effect, as I gave them: (1) a measurement that can show whether the kit
helps: tasks with room to improve, a stronger agent model, planted temptations to count what the guard stops;
(2) more decision power per GPU-hour in the loop: the same seeds compared as pairs, seeds added only when a
result is close, clearly losing runs stopped early; (3) a wider search at low cost: successive halving, and
the search on where it measured better; (4) data and evaluation as changes the loop can keep or revert; (5) a
gate before a long run as one command; (6) confinement on native Windows and macOS; (7) attacking the guard
by machine, with a marker in a sealed file; (8) verifying what is built and unproven: a second reviewer for
round 5's fixes, tests on Linux, macOS and Windows runners at every push, one live Codex and one live Cursor
session; (9) Mac support; (10) remote GPUs one can rely on; (11) robustness of long runs; (12) a view of a
campaign without reading logs; (13) the ledger's open rows, by cheap trials; (14) releases; (15) the guard's
speed. By effect per effort I named item 8 and the small Mac fixes first. This round is item 9, the workflow
of item 8 and, by way of the zsh finding, a part of what item 7 would look for. Item 2's pairing of seeds was
measured in round 2 and rejected at three seeds ("Round 2", point 6); it would have to be measured again with
more seeds before it is built.

### The guard and zsh
The guard reads a shell line as a POSIX shell takes it, a second time as other shells take it (round 5), and
since this round a third time with the patterns of zsh and ksh written as patterns it already knows:

| On the line | Read as | Needs in zsh | In bash |
|---|---|---|---|
| a group of plain names inside a name: `data/(test\|x)/f`, `data/te(st)/f`, `@(a\|b)` | a brace list, `data/{test,x}/f`, or the name itself | nothing; `@(..)` needs `kshglob` | `@(..)` with `extglob` |
| any other group: a pattern inside (`data/(t*\|x)/f`), `!(a)`, `+(a)`, `?(a)` | `*` | nothing for a plain group; `kshglob` for a group with a character in front | `extglob`, for those with a character in front |
| `[^a]` | `[!a]` | nothing | nothing |
| `^name` in a path: `data/^train/f` | `*` | `extendedglob` | |
| `pattern~other` | `pattern` | `extendedglob` | |
| a flag: `data/(#i)TEST/f`, `(#a1)` | every folder name of the word as `*` | `extendedglob` | |

A pair of parentheses counts as a group only where the line cannot mean a subshell, a case pattern or a call
in program text: where more of the name follows right behind it, where it lists alternatives or is `!(..)`
and a name touches it, or where it holds a plain name in front of a `/` or behind one. Quoted text and the
text behind `python -c` are held out before the patterns are read, so a regular expression in quotes keeps
its meaning. The reading only adds answers: a line that was refused or asked about is so still.

Still read as the characters they are, each behind an option that the line or the user's shell settings
would have to switch on: zsh's `x#` (repeats, as in `data/tes#t`), a `^name` that is a whole word (`cd data;
cat ^train`) or stands inside a name (`te^x`), a group without `|` that ends a word (`data/te(st)`, a group
only under `nobareglobqual`), and a pattern under an option that ignores case (`nocaseglob`). A name put
together from variables passes, as before. In the other direction a flag makes the guard refuse more than
the shell would match: `cat data/(#i)TRAIN.csv` is read as `cat data/*` and refused.

### Things to know
- **The public version and your real install have the holes of point 2.** Both get the fix only on your
  word: a push, and a seventh installer run.
- **A push starts the workflow.** It runs six jobs on GitHub's runners at every push and pull request, of
  at most an hour each, free for a public repository. It may only read the repository, and the two actions
  it uses are pinned to commits. The first run may show failures on macOS, which is what it is for. Python
  3.15 is less of a risk than it was: two pre-releases of it pass here.
- **Two interpreters were installed for that pre-check.** uv put Python 3.15.0rc3 (Windows) and 3.15.0b3
  (WSL) into its own folders, where the other test interpreters already lie. On Windows it also put a
  launcher for the new interpreter into the user's `.local\bin`, which I removed again.
- **An older limit of the guard, found in passing and not changed.** The guard asks about a shell command
  that names a frozen or harness file only where the line holds one of its write verbs (a redirect, `tee`,
  `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `sed -i`, `truncate`, `dd`, a few more, and their PowerShell forms). A write by a
  program outside that list passes without a question, on round 5's guard and on the new one alike. Of
  thirteen lines that write a frozen file, ten passed: `sort -o eval/metrics.py data/train.csv`, `curl -o`,
  `wget -O`, `patch`, `install`, `touch`, `black`, `python gen.py --out eval/metrics.py`, PowerShell's
  `Invoke-WebRequest -OutFile`, and `git apply fix.diff`, which names no file. Three were asked about:
  `truncate`, and two `git` lines that fetch the file from another commit. Five lines of the same kind for a
  harness file passed as well, among them `curl -o .claude/nn-training.json URL`, which would replace the
  file that names the sealed paths. The edit tools are asked about. The loop checksums the protected files
  at every iteration, so a campaign notices such a change; an interactive session does not. More verbs
  would narrow the gap and add questions about harmless lines: the rule asks about
  `python eval/metrics.py > out.txt` today, because of the redirect. And a program that names no file, such
  as a formatter run over a folder or a script of the agent's own, is seen by no list. The complete answer
  is a hash of the frozen files in each run's record, which the ledger holds as a Trial row since 11
  November (note `sweep-agent-platform`). I built neither in a round about the Mac, and put the choice to
  you ("What needs your decision", item 4).
- **`caffeinate` holds off idle sleep only.** A closed lid still puts a Mac to sleep, and so does a battery
  that runs low. Its process ends with the run, the loop or the controller it watches.
- **On a Mac the loop refuses `--max-gpu-hours`**, because it measures them with `nvidia-smi`; `--max-hours`
  and `--max-runs` work. The two benchmark tasks train on the CPU there.
- **The container image `alpine:3` is still in WSL's Docker** (a few megabytes, pulled for the shell
  checks). `docker rmi alpine:3` removes it.
- **A seventh installer run on your real install** would add the line `.DS_Store` to the kit's block of its
  `.gitignore` and bring the new guard and scripts. On Windows nothing else of this round acts.

### Not done, and why
- **A box for the loop's runs on macOS** (the review's finding 4): point 3 says why. The design, for whoever
  has a Mac. Translate the bubblewrap arguments that `sandbox()` and `eval_box()` in `nnloop.py` already
  compose into a Seatbelt profile, so that the Linux path does not change: `--unshare-net` becomes
  `(deny network*)` with allowances for unix sockets, which PyTorch's data workers may need (localhost stays
  closed, where a run on Linux has a loopback of its own); `--ro-bind R R` becomes `(deny file-write*
  (subpath R))`; `--tmpfs D` and `--ro-bind /dev/null F`, which hide sealed data, become `(deny file-read*
  (subpath D))` and `(deny file-read* (literal F))`; `--bind W W` becomes `(allow file-write* (subpath W))`.
  Paths go in as the kernel names them (`/private/var/...`, and in the case the disk has). The profile runs
  as `sandbox-exec -f <file>`. Before a campaign the box must prove itself inside the real profile, as the
  bubblewrap box does: a hidden path refuses to be read, a connection to a socket the loop listens on at
  127.0.0.1 fails, a write in the project fails, a write in the runs folder succeeds; if any of it does not
  hold, the loop runs unconfined as today and says so. The sandbox checks of `tests/test_loop.py` (section
  12) test behaviour, not bubblewrap, and would run on a Mac with one assertion adapted. Then one training
  run on the Apple GPU inside the box, which no hosted runner can stand in for. A campaign started without
  the box cannot be resumed with it: the loop refuses changed conditions. Ledger: a Trial row of the note
  `round6`.
- **The `mps` device in the kit's own tools**: a row in `expctl env --probe`, the memory figures of a run's
  heartbeat, the device choice of the two benchmark tasks. None could be run here, and code for a device
  that never ran is a guess. Ledger: Trial.
- **A field for the device a run used**, and a refusal to compare runs of different devices: the open half
  of the row "Apple-silicon notes and a backend field in run records", which stays unfinished.
- **mlx-lm for fine-tuning on a Mac**: named as a candidate in the reference's section, not tried. Ledger:

- **Keep-awake on Windows and Linux**: not built; the row of 11 November stays undecided.
- **The path forms under `/private`**: not looked at. The workflow's macOS jobs run the tests in temporary
  folders under `/var/folders`, which will show it. Ledger: Assess.
- **The guard's limits of "The guard and zsh"**: each needs a shell option. Closing them by reading takes
  knowing the user's shell options, which the guard cannot; a sandbox is the tool for that.
- **The guard's list of write verbs**: found, recorded and put to you ("Things to know"). Ledger: Trial.
- **No reviewer without the working context looked at this round.** Its guard change is 63 lines; my check

## Round 7 (14 and 15 November 2026): a second review, checked claim by claim

After round 6 you gave me a second reviewer's report on the public version (`bc96015`) and asked for the best
plan from it and for the plan's execution. The report is kept out of git
(`docs/upgrade/scout/scouts/user-review-1114b.md`). It has three parts: findings about the code, an audit for
the Mac, and a design of its own ("v2.0") against which it scores the kit. I took its claims as leads: each
was checked against the code, and run where a run was cheap, before anything was built. The order of the work
was: defects that weaken the sealed test set, the frozen evaluator or the protection of live runs; then a
check that finds such defects without a reviewer; then the proposals. The scores against "v2.0" were not a
goal. This section is that work: nine commits, `e777e0b` to `4d0d543`, on top of round 6's, and the commit of
these records. Nothing is pushed. Nothing was run, read or changed on your real install. **Nothing of this
round has run on macOS.**

Since then: on your "Push test branch" of 15 November this round is on the public branch `test/rounds-6-7`
and, on your "Push main" of the same day, on `main`, and its tests have run on GitHub's macOS, Linux and
Windows runners. Where this section says that nothing is pushed, that nothing ran on a Mac or that the
workflow has never run, "The test branch" (the next section) has what is true now; where it says that a
seventh installer run on your real install was not made, it was made on 15 November (the last part of that
section). The rest of the section stands as it was written.

### In short
1. **The report's claim about the evaluator is wrong, and its findings about the guard and the controller are
   right.** It said that the benchmark's evaluator runs code from a model file through `torch.jit.load`. I
   built 36 such files, each with one pickle entry swapped for a payload, and loaded them with the installed
   PyTorch 2.9.1: no payload ran. A test now asks the installed PyTorch again at every run of the tests. The
   evaluator is unchanged. Right, each confirmed before the change and fixed with a test: four ways to write a
   frozen file or read a sealed one past the guard (`644b2c9`), and three faults in the controller
   (`78b1a17`): `expctl stop` signalled a recorded process number without checking whose it had become, the
   record of the final evaluation was appended to without a lock (six writers at once lost 91 of 240 rows on
   Windows and broke the chain in WSL), and two remote bookings made at the same moment both gave up.
2. **The guard now has a test that looks for holes by itself, and its first run found many.**
   `tests/test_guard_live.py` builds command lines from parts (what is done, how the path is written, what
   the command is wrapped in), asks the guard about each, and gives every line that the guard lets pass to a
   real shell in a temporary project. A line that passed must not have printed or copied the sealed file or
   changed the frozen file. Before any fix, 185 of 901 lines that passed in bash did one of the three (seed
   11, 2,100 lines). Most were writes of the frozen file; a few read the sealed file. Each kind is now either
   closed in the guard with a hand-written case, or named as a limit in `docs/REFERENCE.md` and left out of
   the generator ("The generated test"). About a third of the lines pass the guard.
3. **An independent review then found fifteen faults in the round as I had first finished it, and all are
   fixed** (`0aafe9a`, `439ab60`). At `eb73521` the generated test was clean in five shells, and I called the
   guard's part done. A reviewer with no view of my work found nine further kinds of line that passed the
   guard and printed the sealed file or changed the frozen file: a code flag in a group of letters
   (`sh -ce '…'`), a bracket in quotes inside `$(…)`, a program's name in capitals, `git checkout -q .`,
   `sort -uo`, a search that feeds a `while read` loop, and others. The test had not seen them, because its
   parts did not build them. The guard reads them now, the parts build them, and the larger samples that
   followed found 16 more lines of three causes, closed as well. On the final state no line that passed did
   harm, among 15,600 generated: bash in WSL (three seeds of 2,100 lines), bash and zsh 5.9 in an Alpine
   container (two seeds of 1,200 lines each), Git's bash (two seeds of 1,500) and PowerShell (two seeds of
   750) on Windows. **The lesson holds beyond this round: the test finds what its parts can build and nothing
   else, and a clean sample is not a proof.** The review also found three faults in the controller and five
   harmless lines that this round had turned into questions ("The independent review").
4. **Every run's record now holds a hash of the frozen files** (`adeddcf`; a remote run's since `0aafe9a`).
   The guard asks before a write to a frozen file that it can name, and it cannot name every write (an
   archive unpacked over the evaluator, a program that builds the path while it runs). `expctl launch` and
   `nnremote launch` write `frozen_hash` into the run's manifest, `expctl hash` prints the current one,
   `expctl status` puts an alert first when a ranked run was made under other frozen files than the project
   holds now, and the final evaluation's receipt carries the hash. `expctl selftest` also compares the
   installed kit files with the hashes in the install manifest.
5. **The price: the guard asks in more cases.** A copy out of a folder that holds frozen files
   (`cp -r eval sub/copy`), an error stream sent to a file beside a frozen file (`python eval/metrics.py 2>
   err.txt`), a formatter or fixer over a folder with frozen files (`black .`, `ruff check --fix .`), a
   search that feeds an edit (`ls *.py | xargs black`), cmd's `for /r` wherever sealed files lie below, a
   word in capitals that is a program's name beside a kept file. In an unattended session each of these
   questions is a refusal. "Changes in the behaviour of existing features" lists every changed answer.
6. **The front page and the banner said more than was measured**, as the report noted: the gain they named
   comes from one campaign. They say so now (`e777e0b`). Round 6 had already added the commands that were
   missing from the reference.
7. **The report's design is not built.** Ten training back ends behind one recipe file, a search plane, a
   campaign run by several agents and a restructure into a package are rejected, each with its reason in the
   ledger; five further proposals wait for something this machine does not have (a Mac, a rented machine, a
   second GPU, agent sessions). "Not done, and why" has the list.

The report's Mac audit repeats points that round 6 built (the process start time without `/proc`, the Finder
file, `caffeinate`, zsh). Two of its Mac proposals have ledger rows: `caffeinate -dimsu` is rejected (a run
needs the system awake, which `-i` gives), and a report of Metal's wired-memory limit waits for a Mac. Its
claims about versions, papers and other tools that no change depends on were not checked.

### The generated test
- **What it is.** `tests/test_guard_live.py`, the eighth test file. Bash and zsh lines come from 67 ways to
  read, 51 ways to write, Python one-liners, 34 spellings of a path (quotes, wildcards, variables, `$PWD`,
  case on a file system that ignores it; 41 under zsh, with its own patterns) and 46 wrappers (a subshell, a
  function, `bash -c` with its flag in a group or behind options, `eval`, a here-document, `trap`, a variable
  that is run, `$(…)` with a bracket in quotes, Python's `os.system`); PowerShell lines from its own parts
  (aliases, cmd, provider paths, script blocks, an encoded command). One line in seven names only the folder
  above the file. There are two frozen files, because the first one's name (`eval/metrics.py`) holds words
  that the guard reads as runners, which hid misses; the second is `scoring/rules.txt`. The same parts are
  also used on files that nothing protects, and nine in ten of those lines must pass: a guard that asked
  about everything would fail there. In the samples below, 98 to 100 in 100 passed.
- **The judge is the shell.** Each line that passed runs in a temporary project whose sealed file holds a
  marker. The test looks for the marker in the output (plain, reversed, hex, base64) and in every file, and
  compares the frozen files. Before it trusts the judge it gives it one line that prints the sealed file and
  one that changes the frozen file. The project is put back after every line that changed it.
- **Where it runs.** bash in WSL and in an Alpine container, zsh 5.9 in that container, Git's bash and
  PowerShell on Windows. The sample comes from a fixed seed (7, 150 lines of each kind), so the suite's run
  repeats; `python tests/test_guard_live.py SEED COUNT` takes another sample.
- **The samples on the final state (`439ab60`), each line that passed run in its shell, none harmful:**

  | Shell | Seeds × lines | Passed the guard | Harmless lines that passed |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | bash 5.2.21 in WSL | 5, 7, 311 × 2,100 | 707, 701, 708 | 694, 688, 695 of 700 |
  | bash 5.3.9 in `alpine:3` | 7, 5 × 1,200 | 403, 406 | 396, 400 of 400 |
  | zsh 5.9 in `alpine:3` | 7, 5 × 1,200 | 402, 404 | 395, 399 of 400 |
  | Git's bash 5.2.37 on Windows | 7, 311 × 1,500 | 504, 503 | 496, 499 of 500 |
  | PowerShell 7.7.0 on Windows | 7, 311 × 750 | 258, 261 | 250, 250 of 250 |

- **What it does not show.** A sample, not a proof, and only of what its parts build. Twice in this round a
  clean sample was followed by a find: a sixth bash seed found `(git checkout HEAD .)` after five clean
  ones, and the independent review found nine kinds of line at a commit where every sample was clean. The
  same samples with the review's forms in the parts then found 16 different harmful lines before the last
  fixes (counting a line once for each sample that held it: bash 9 in 6,300 in WSL and 2 in 2,400 in the
  container, zsh 4 in 2,400, Git's bash 5 in 3,000, PowerShell none in 1,500). Another seed, or another
  reader, may find more. It has not run under macOS's zsh or bash 3.2; the workflow will run it there at the
  first push. It does not judge live runs.

### Changes in the behaviour of existing features
**The guard, first part (`644b2c9`). Each was allowed before and is asked about now**, where the line names a
frozen or harness file, a file in `.git`, or the folder of an active run:
- a write by pathlib's one-argument `.rename(` and `.replace(`, by `.touch(`, `.symlink_to(`,
  `.hardlink_to(`, `.link_to(`, and by `os.truncate`, `os.link`, `os.symlink`;
- the word behind an output option: `-o`, `-O`, `--out…`, PowerShell's `-OutFile`, also attached
  (`--out…=FILE`, `-OutFile:FILE`, `-oFILE`). A line without a write verb is judged by that word alone;
- `touch`, `patch`, `install` where a command starts;
- `black`, `isort`, `ruff format` without `--check` or `--diff`;
- a notes file run through zsh's `=(…)`; and the text of a zsh glob qualifier `e` gets the answer of the
  command it holds;
- a filtered search where a wildcard seal's walk is cut by the hook's time (was: no answer);
- for read-only agents, `touch`, `patch`, `install` and the pathlib forms are refused (was: no answer).

Reason: each wrote a frozen file or read a sealed one past the guard, confirmed by a run. Tests: cases in
`tests/test_kit.py`, among them lines that must stay without a question (`str.replace(a, b)`, `grep -o`,
`--output-dir runs/new --config eval/metrics.py`, `black --check`, `echo touch eval/metrics.py`,
`ls *(.om[1])`, `sort -o sub/sorted.csv data/train.csv`).

**The guard, second part (`eb73521`), found by the generated test.** Asked about now, allowed before, unless
the entry says otherwise:
1. A frozen or harness file, a file in `.git` or an active run's folder on a line with a redirection behind a
   descriptor or `&` (`1>`, `2>`, `&>`, `1>>`, `>& file`; not `2>&1`, not one to `/dev/null`, `$null` or
   `nul`).
2. `sed --in-place`, and sed's `-i` wherever it stands.
3. `git checkout <rev> <path>` and `git restore <path>` count as writes of the path; `git checkout <rev> .`
   is a destructive git operation, also where a bracket or a quote follows the dot
   (`(git checkout HEAD .)`).
4. `find … -delete` is a write.
5. Python's `open()` whose path is a call inside a call, and `.open('w')` behind a bracket.
6. The text of `trap '…' SIGNAL` gets the answer of the command it holds.
7. A command whose output the line takes in (`$(…)`, backticks) is read as a command of its own, also inside
   a string in double quotes, where quoting starts anew. A here-document that no program runs stays unread,
   so a commit message may hold anything. **One existing expectation changed with this:**
   `echo "$(<data/test/labels.csv)"` was asked about and is now refused, like `cat` of the same file.
8. `${name:-word}`, `${name-word}`, `${name:=word}` and `${name:+word}` are read as `word`.
9. `git ls-files` is a reader like `git grep`. With `-o` and no `--exclude-standard`, or with `-i`, it lists
   what git ignores, and is asked about where sealed files lie below the folder it runs in.
10. A write verb inside text handed to a shell counts for the paths of the outer line
    (`f=eval/metrics.py bash -c 'rm "$f"'`).
11. A new question, "Command changes a whole folder, or the files that it finds there itself, and files that
    this guard keeps lie in it": `mv`, `rm -r`, `git mv`, `rsync`, `cp -r`, `Remove-Item -Recurse` and the
    like over a folder that holds frozen or harness files, on either side of a copy; `find … -delete` or an
    edit fed by a search of the same line (`| xargs`, `$(…)`, `-exec`, PowerShell's pipe into `Remove-Item`,
    `Set-Content` and their short forms) over such a folder, with the search's file filter respected; and a
    formatter that is given such a folder or none.
12. `ruff --fix`, `ruff check --fix` and `--unsafe-fixes` (not with `--diff`) count as a formatter.
13. Text nested in text is read three levels deep (was two); a fourth level is asked about.
14. A text that the line keeps in a variable (`c='rm x'; $c`, `$c = 'del x'; iex $c`) is read as a command
    where the line has something that runs text, or the variable stands where a command starts.
15. PowerShell: the text of `[scriptblock]::Create('…')` is read as a command, and so is the text behind
    `iex` or `Invoke-Expression` inside a block without blanks (`&{iex '…'}`, `try{iex '…'}catch{}`). A
    path with the block's closing bracket on it is read without the bracket (`&{del eval\m*.py}`).
16. cmd's `for /r` is a recursive command: asked about where sealed files lie below the folder the line runs
    in, also when it names a folder without them (the guard does not read which folder it walks).
17. For read-only agents, the new write verbs, the formatters and a `trap` text that writes are refused (was:
    no answer).

Reason for each: a generated line of that kind passed the guard and did the harm in a real shell. Tests: a
hand-written case for each in `tests/test_kit.py` (the blocks that begin "a folder that holds frozen or
harness files" and "a text that the line keeps in a variable"), with the lines that must stay without a
question beside them; the read-only cases in `tests/test_review_fixes.py`, section 10; and the generated test
itself.

**The guard, third part (`439ab60`): what the independent review found, and what the generated test found once
its parts held the review's forms.** Asked about now (refused where the line reaches sealed data), allowed
before, unless the entry says otherwise:
1. The text behind a code flag wherever the flag stands: in a group of letters (`sh -ce '…'`, `bash -xc '…'`,
   `perl -ne '…'`), cut short as PowerShell allows (`powershell -com "…"`), and with options or `--` between
   the flag and the text (`bash -c -- '…'`, `bash -c -o pipefail '…'`, `trap -- '…' EXIT`). Every word of an
   `eval` is read, also behind a separator that the line escapes (`eval : \; 'rm …'`); not where `eval` is a
   folder that `-C`, `--chdir`, `--directory` or `--cwd` names.
2. A command inside `$(…)` ends where a shell ends it: a bracket in quotes, a pattern of `case` and what
   follows a here-document no longer cut it short. Its words in single quotes are read as they stand; they
   were blanked, so `echo "$(python -c "open('eval/metrics.py', 'w')")"` passed.
3. Variables: `${@:-word}` and `${:-word}` are read as `word`; a variable set from another (`d=$c; $d`); a
   one-word text where a command starts (`c="rm"; $c file`, `$c = 'del'; & $c file`); zsh's `${=c}`, `$=c`,
   `${(z)c}`, `${~c}` and `${(e)c}`.
4. PowerShell: `[Any.Namespace.ScriptBlock]::Create('…')`, the engine's `.InvokeScript('…')`,
   `.NewScriptBlock(` and `.AddScript(`; a file object's own `.Delete()`, `.MoveTo(` and `.CopyTo(`.
5. Program text that hands a command to a shell (`os.system('…')`, `subprocess.run([…])`, `popen`, the
   `exec` and `spawn` calls): the command gets its own answer, with the string read as Python reads it
   (`\'`, `\\`, `\n`) and as it stands.
6. zsh: a group with a wildcard beside a slash (`cat dat?/(tes?)/lab*`), and a qualifier `e` whose delimiter
   is a letter.
7. A program's name in any case (`RM`, `SED`, `CP`, `Rmdir`, `GREP -r`, `FIND`, `KILL`, `GIT`), and
   `git.exe`: Windows finds a program so, and so does a Mac as it comes.
8. `git checkout` with options before the path (`git checkout -q .`), with `./`, `:/` or a wildcard for the
   path, and `git checkout --force`; `git restore --staged --worktree` and `-SW`.
9. Writes: perl's and ruby's `-i` wherever it stands, BSD sed's `-I`; an output letter that ends a group
   (`sort -uo`, `curl -sSLo`, `wget -qO`); an output word that is a wildcard (it counts as what it names on
   disk), a variable or a command's output (then every path of the line may be the one written). Reads:
   `diff -r` and `git diff --no-index` over a folder with sealed files.
10. A search that feeds a loop (`… | while read f; do sed -i … "$f"; done`, `done < <(…)`,
    `for f in $(…)`), also where the loop writes by a redirect into its variable; a search that feeds `cp` or
    `dd`; PowerShell's block with a write anywhere in it or a redirect into a variable, and
    `foreach (…) { … }`.
11. A formatter behind the runner that starts it: `uvx`, `pipx run`, `uv tool run`, `conda run -n env`,
    `python -m`, `black@24.1.0`. The wrappers `setsid` and `caffeinate` are seen through.
12. **Allowed again.** The second part had made these questions, and each was allowed before this round:
    `black --version`, `black --help`, `isort -c .`, `git restore --staged <file>`, `python -O <file>`,
    `ls -lo <file>`, and a line with the shell's own `eval` beside a delete or a move of another file.
13. For read-only agents the same forms are refused (was: no answer): a program's name in capitals, perl's
    `-i`, a formatter behind a runner, a code flag in a group, `os.system('…')`, `git checkout -q .`.

Reason for 1 to 11 and 13: the reviewer, or the generated test after it, had a line of that kind which passed
the guard and did the harm in a real shell ("The independent review"). Reason for 12: harmless lines that
this round had turned into questions. Tests: hand-written cases in `tests/test_kit.py` (the block that begins
"were None, each of them (the review of round 7", with the lines that must stay without a question below
it), `tests/test_review_fixes.py` sections 9 and 10, and the generated test, whose parts now build these
forms. Against the public version, no existing case that expected a question or a refusal was changed to
expect none.

**The controller.**
- `expctl stop` signals the supervisor only while the start time (or key) in the launch record still matches
  the process; otherwise it stops the run through the run's own process. A record from before this round has
  neither: there the process's start is compared with the record's launch time (`0aafe9a`; in `78b1a17` such a
  record was taken as the same process, which the review found).
- The record of the final evaluation is written under a file lock (flock, a byte lock on Windows). Of two
  final evaluations started at the same moment, one runs and the other gets the single-use refusal; its
  attempt stays in the receipt and counts as a use (`0aafe9a`; both ran before, and within one second their
  rows counted as one use). Start and end rows carry a `nonce` for this. With `--again` both run, each with
  its stated reason.
- `nnremote.reserve()`: of two bookings that the cap cannot both cover, the earlier row in the ledger holds
  and the later one gives way. Before, both gave up.
- A run's manifest has three new fields (`frozen_hash`, `frozen_files`, `frozen_size_only`), `expctl hash`
  (an older command) prints the same three for the project as it stands, `expctl status` can begin with an
  alert about changed frozen files (the ranking itself is not filtered), and `expctl selftest` has one more
  line, which is not a required check. At most 64 MB are
  read for the hash, the smallest files first; a larger file counts by its size. A text file counts with LF
  line ends, so a checkout that git wrote with CRLF gives the same value as one with LF (`0aafe9a`; the review
  found that the two differed). `nnremote launch` writes the hash into a remote run's manifest too
  (`0aafe9a`). A run started by neither command carries no hash. No path or format changed, so the installer
  migrates nothing.
- The installer is unchanged in this round.

### The independent review
A reviewer with no access to my working context reviewed the round as it stood at `eb73521`: a fresh subagent,
as in the rounds before (the deep-sweep-red-team skill was passed over for its cost). Its brief named the diff
(`fd8c18c..eb73521`), what the guard protects and the limits that `docs/REFERENCE.md` names, and told it not
to read these records. It read the code, asked the guard at both commits about some 330 lines of its own, ran
50 of them in a real shell in a throwaway project, and ran the generated test once with its own seed. It kept
15 findings, 11 marked certain and 4 likely. **Nine of them (1 to 9) were ways past the sealed test set or the
frozen evaluator at the commit I had called clean, and the generated test did not see them, because its parts
did not build them.** All 15 are fixed in code, each with a test; none is answered by argument alone.

| 2 | `$(…)` with a bracket in quotes, or with a command behind a here-document (certain) | Fixed; entry 2. Not by the fix it proposed (read all up to the line's last bracket): the guard now ends `$(…)` where a shell does |

**What the fixes then showed.** With its new parts the generated test found 16 more harmful lines in about
14,000 (three causes: words in single quotes inside `$(…)`, Python's own escapes in `os.system('…')`, an
output word given by backticks), and my own probes found two (`eval` with an escaped separator, a loop that
writes by a redirect). All are fixed with hand-written cases (entries 1, 2, 5, 9 and 10). The samples on the
final state are in "The generated test".

**The reviewer's own lines.** Of the 50 lines that it ran in a shell, 47 are asked about or refused now. Three
stay allowed, and they are not among its findings: each reads sealed data through a path that a program puts
together while it runs (`pathlib.Path('data').glob('*/*.csv')`, `os.chdir('data')` before a `glob`,

lines cannot close it; what holds against it is a test loader that refuses to load without the unseal

**What it checked and found sound:** about 150 everyday lines answer as before the round, apart from those of

second booking gives way, a third can be refused although it would fit under the cap; that errs on the cap's

**What it could not check, and where that stands now:** zsh, Linux, Python 3.8 and the newest Python: run here

### Things to know
- **What the guard still does not see as a write of a frozen file**, each tried on 14 November and allowed:
  a git command that replaces the working tree as a whole (`git stash`, a change of branch, `pull`, `merge`,
  `rebase`; `git reset --hard` is asked about); an archive unpacked over the file (`tar x`, `unzip`);
  `git apply`; a download that names only its address (`curl -O`); a formatter the guard does not know
  (`autopep8 -i`, `yapf -i`, `prettier --write`); the whole project removed under another spelling of its
  folder; `tee` behind a search, a PowerShell block inside a block, a script that a loop over a search
  starts; and any program that builds the path while it runs. The frozen hash in each run's record is the
  check for these. `docs/REFERENCE.md`, "Notes and limits", has the list.
- **Sealed data read through a path that a program builds while it runs is not seen either** (the three lines
  in "The independent review"). The check for that is not in the guard: a loader that refuses without the
  unseal variable, or test data kept outside the repository.
- **The guard's rules look at the whole line.** With a write on the line, every path of the line may be the
  one written; the search-feeds-edit rule does not ask which search feeds which edit; the whole-folder rule
  does not tell a copy's source from its target. So harmless lines are asked about: a word in capitals that
  is a program's name (`RM`, `CP`, `DD`, `TEE`) beside a kept file, a restore of another file beside one,
  `note='rm -rf runs/old'; python -c "print(1)"`.
- **The rule for read-only agents does not read output options** (`sort -o notes.txt notes.txt` passes it; a
  frozen or harness file there is still asked about by the guard's own rule). Reading them would refuse
  `grep -o`. It has been so since the rule exists.
- **A frozen hash that a run recorded on a checkout with CRLF line ends before `0aafe9a`** differs from the one
  computed now. None is public: the hash is from this round.
- **The frozen hash costs time for each frozen file, not only for each byte.** Measured on Windows on
  15 November with the tests running beside it, best of three: 64 MB in 64 files 0.1 s; 400 files of 1 MB
  0.15 s (64 read, 336 by their size); 5,000 files of 2 KB 2.3 s; 20,000 files of 1 KB 8.7 s. In WSL, on its
  own file system, the last two took 0.16 s and 0.69 s, which points at what Windows charges for opening a
  file (not looked into further).
  `expctl launch`, `expctl hash` and the final evaluation pay it each time, `expctl status` and the status at
  a session's start once a ranked run carries a hash. That hook has 30 s, so on Windows, with a frozen data
  folder of some 60,000 files or more (my extrapolation, not a run), the status at a session's start may not
  arrive. The guard's protection of those files does not depend on it. A bound on the number of files read
  is not the answer: the smallest files are read first, and an evaluator beside 20,000 smaller data files
  would fall outside it. Not measured on an idle machine.

  lock test's files, a copy of a test runner); the container image `alpine:3` in WSL's Docker.

## The test branch (15 November 2026): the tests on GitHub's Linux, macOS and Windows machines

After round 7 I asked whether to push rounds 6 and 7 to a test branch, so that the workflow runs the tests on
GitHub's macOS, Linux and Windows machines, and you answered "Push test branch". I had said what a yes
covers: the push of this work to the public repository under a test name, follow-up pushes to that branch to
repair what fails, and the six jobs that each push starts there (free for a public repository), while `main`
stays. This section is that work: the push of round 7's last commit, `9d2ff12`, as the branch
`test/rounds-6-7`; three commits for what the first run showed (`bd8350e`, `70b137e`, `97b3211`) and their
push; and, after the second run, a correction of one page of the kit (`1578bd0`) and the commit of these
records, pushed to the same branch. During this work `main` stayed at `bc96015`; what you then decided for
it is the last part of this section ("`main`"). There is no pull request. Nothing was run, read or changed
on your real install.

### In short
1. **The kit's tests pass on a Mac, on bare Linux and on a Windows that may create symlinks.** Second run of
   the workflow, commit `97b3211`: all six jobs pass, 1,460 to 1,470 checks each, with no third-party
   package. Until this day the tests had run on one machine, on native Windows and in WSL2.
2. **The first run failed in four of six jobs, and one of its three causes was a fault of the kit.** A
   project may hold a relative link to one of its own folders. A snapshot makes such a link again, and on
   Windows it made it as a link to a file, because Windows fixes a link's kind when the link is made and the
   folder it names is copied after it. The link then opened nothing. In a project that is not a git
   repository the next step asked whether that name exists, which on Python 3.8 ended the launch with "Access
   is denied"; on Python 3.15 nothing was reported and the link stayed wrong. It did not show on this machine,
   whose Windows account may not create symlinks, so that a snapshot here holds junctions and hard links and
   this code had never run on Windows. Fixed in `bd8350e`, with the check that found it extended.
3. **The other two causes lay in tests.** One test compared the project folder that `expctl` hands to a run,
   which `expctl` resolves, with the unresolved name of its temporary folder; GitHub's Windows names that
   folder in a short form and macOS reaches it through a link, so two checks failed in all four jobs. Another
   found files in a stand-in home directory after the installer's runs, under macOS's own Python only. The
   kit was right in both cases (`70b137e`).
4. **The generated guard test met macOS's own shells for the first time**: bash 3.2.57 and zsh 5.9. Of 450
   generated lines the guard let 150 and 148 pass, and none of them printed or copied the sealed file or
   changed the frozen file. The same holds for the other shells of the six jobs.
5. **What has still not run on a Mac:** an agent session; training, because the runners have no PyTorch, so
   nothing ran on the Apple GPU; sleep and a closed lid; a box for the loop's runs, which is not built. The
   runner is a virtual machine (`expctl env` read 7 GB and "Apple M1 (Virtual)"), not a Mac that a person
   uses.
6. **`main` did not have rounds 6 and 7 while this work ran, and has them since your "Push main" of the same
   day** ("`main`", near the end of this section). On your real install the guard's holes that those
   rounds closed stayed open until the seventh installer run of that day ("The seventh installer run on
   the real install").

## Round 8 (15 and 16 November 2026): a third review, checked claim by claim

After the seventh installer run you gave me a third reviewer's report, written on the public version
(`fb101a7`), and asked for the project to be upgraded further on its recommendations, as well as possible.
The report is kept out of git (`docs/upgrade/scout/scouts/user-review-1115.md`). It has three parts: six
findings about the code, five "pillars" of proposals that make up a design of its own ("v2-lean", which it
scores at 97 of 100), and closing instructions to its reader: to copy a prompt, which the pasted text does
not hold, into a session on a new branch, or to start a plan or a team of agents, and to land its first
phase first. I took it as I took the two reviews before it: its claims are leads. Each was checked against
the code, and by a run where a run was cheap, before anything was changed; each proposal was decided on
evidence and has a ledger row; its instructions were not followed, and its score was not a goal. The result
then went to readers without my working context, and what they found is fixed or answered below. This
section is that work: 24 commits from `703f074` to `8fbec1c`, and the commit that holds this section.
Nothing was pushed when the round ended, and nothing of it had run on macOS or on GitHub's machines. On
your "Push test branch" of 16 November it went to a public test branch, where all six jobs pass: "The test
branch of round 8", the section after this one. Where this section says that nothing is pushed, or that
something has run on WSL2 only, that section is the later word. Nothing was run, read or changed on your
real install, and no agent session was started.

### In short
1. **All six of the report's findings held at least in part.** Most were narrower than stated; the one on
   large frozen files held in full, and the one on the margin held further than I first recorded. Each is
   fixed as far as it held, with a test:
   - One refused call no longer costs an unattended iteration when the call is routine: an undo with git, or
     a formatter given a folder (`d7265c8`). Every other refusal still voids the iteration, among them a
     forced `git clean` aimed at a file or folder that the guard keeps (`f429101`).
   - The guard no longer asks about a line that only sends an evaluator's output to a file (`python
     eval/metrics.py > score.json`): it reads the redirection's target as the written file (`703f074`).
     **This is the one change of the round that makes the guard ask less.** "Changes in the behaviour of
     existing features" has its conditions.
   - A remote launch holds the spending ledger's lock from its read to its write (`6450d1c`). The report's
     stronger claim, that the cap could be passed, did not hold in a run.
   - Every frozen file counts with its content, however large (`6cd4ee3`). Before, a change in the middle of
     a frozen file of more than 64 MB left the hash of the frozen files and the loop's checksum as they
     were, and a frozen base model is such a file. My first fix left two ways around it, which the
     independent review found and which are closed (`e451124`, `e334c3a`).
   - The benchmark saves a model that was trained under `torch.compile` (`1afc9d1`, `81ffe3a`).
   - After a near-miss's second look, the margin for the next changes is no longer 13 % too small
     (`1fe37fd`). Of the report's two figures for the harm, one is borne out for the rule as it was, and
     the other may count something I had counted otherwise ("The report's findings, one by one").
2. **The independent review at the end found more than the report had.** Three readers without my context
   were asked. The reader of the controller and the loop kept 19 findings, and ranked seven above the
   rest: under WSL2 a run in the loop's sandbox could read the sealed data through the system's second
   mount of the disk, start a Windows program, and write anywhere outside the project; hours given as "NaN"
   switched the spending cap off for every later launch; a run could forge the records by which the
   harness ends and stops runs; the kept hash of a large frozen file could be planted; a folder sealed by
   its full path was half sealed; and two more of that kind. Four of the 19 sat in code older than this
   round. The reader of my claims and decisions kept 14, among them two verdicts of mine that were wrong
   (the rejection of the report's variance formula, and "compiling did not pay") and one that was too mild
   (the margin). All 33 are fixed or answered ("The independent review"). **The third reader, for the
   guard, was stopped by the model's safeguards before it reported, and I did not redo its work in this
   session: the guard's changes of this round have had no independent reading of their own.**
   (On 16 November they got one, from a reader with another brief: "The second reading of the guard's
   changes of round 8". It found two regressions in `703f074`, which are fixed there.)
3. **Built from the report's proposals.** A training run in the loop's sandbox has a process namespace of
   its own, so it can no longer see or signal a process outside it (`c858226`; round 5 had left this open
   with the test it needed). The worker's prompt says where the last run of a discarded change ended
   (`1933688`). A test split kept in a folder outside the project is sealed under either spelling of its
   name, which failed for a full path (`53838a6`, `8dcc12f`). The fine-tuning reference has a smoke run
   before RL post-training (`2947666`).
4. **One of the report's methods was measured instead of adopted on its word, and it won.** Muon for the
   2-D weights inside the blocks, beside AdamW for the rest, against AdamW alone at its best rate, on the
   kit's character-model benchmark: 1.6483 against 1.6748 nats per character on the loop's validation split
   (three seeds, runs of 30 s), a difference of 0.0265, which is a t of 3.6 with about 4 degrees of freedom,
   although a Muon step cost 1.84 times as much. `references/optimization.md` now names it as the first
   challenger once AdamW is tuned, for a transformer trained from scratch (`6f4769e`, `dc4fcd6`). It is not
   a default: one small task, one machine, three seeds, a repeat that moved Muon's score by more than its
   spread across seeds, and no control with matched update size ("What was measured").
5. **Most of the report's design is not built, each part with its reason in the ledger.** Rejected: six
   starter packs that would make defaults of methods the kit holds untested; a second archive slot for
   faster or leaner changes; two refinements of the loop's search; a command that moves sealed data, with
   the guard eased on the strength of the place; a guard that lets a comment naming a sealed path pass; one
   model load per evaluation. On hold: a guard that judges each command of a line by itself; a forecasting
   model wired into a pack. Undecided, each with the test it needs: the report's variance formula over
   seeds and items as the keep rule's standard error; `torch.export` as the benchmark's model file;
   NVIDIA's Transformer Engine. More of its proposals are decided by rows of earlier rounds, unchanged
   ("The report's proposals").
6. **What this round cannot show.** Whether the worker's new history lines make campaigns end better: that
   needs agent sessions for both arms. Whether anything new holds on a Mac or on bare Linux: nothing was
   pushed, so GitHub's machines have not run it, and the read-only sandbox and the Linux proofs behind a
   stop have run on WSL2 only (answered on 16 November: GitHub's machines ran it, and all of it passes;
   "The test branch of round 8"). Whether Muon's edge holds beyond one small task.

### The report's findings, one by one
"By a run" means that I ran it here; "by reading" means the code only.

| The report's finding | Verdict | What was done |
|---|---|---|
| One refused call voids an unattended iteration and bars its change for the campaign | Confirmed, by reading and by a campaign with the stand-in agent | `d7265c8`: a refusal whose every reason is a git undo or a formatter given a folder with kept files is marked routine; the loop does not void the iteration for it. A change voided only by its session's refused calls is no longer remembered as tried. `f429101`, after the independent review: a forced `git clean` that names a kept file, or a folder that holds one, is not routine |
| The guard asks about harmless lines: an evaluator's output sent to a file, an undo of an unprotected file, a formatter over the project, a comment that names a sealed path | Confirmed by asking the guard about each line, attended and unattended | The redirections pass now (`703f074`). The undo and the formatter are refused as before and no longer void an iteration. The comment stays a question (ledger: Reject; "Things to know") |
| The spending ledger's lock is partial, and launches at the same moment can pass the cap, leave reservations behind or damage a line | In part, by a run with three processes ($4, $4 and $1 against a cap of $5): nothing was held from the read to the write, and outside Windows a row was appended with no lock. Not confirmed: the cap was never passed, and a refused launch left no reservation. No verdict: that two launches which both write without the lock, after 3 s of waiting for it on Windows, damage a line. Such a wait was not produced in a test | `6450d1c`: the lock is held from the read of what is committed to the write of the reservation. After it, six rounds on Windows and six in WSL: one $4 launch and the $1 launch reserve, the other is refused. The fallback after 3 s is kept: a launch reads the ledger again after its write and gives way if its row is missing or came second, and a line that is no ledger row refuses every paid start |
| The hash of the frozen files reads nothing of a file beyond the first 64 MB, and the loop's checksum leaves out the middle of a large file | Confirmed in full, by a run: a change in the middle of such a file changed neither | `6cd4ee3`: every file counts with its content, and the hash of a large file is kept until its size or times change. After the independent review: a launch reads every frozen file and takes no kept hash (`e451124`), and on Windows, where a file has no change time, the loop reads a large protected file in full after every evaluation (`e334c3a`) |
| The benchmark's model file keeps out `torch.compile` and hand-written kernels; the evaluator loads the model again for every batch; code in `__setstate__` runs at load | In part, by runs with PyTorch 2.9.1: a compiled model could not be saved; a hand-written autograd function cannot be in the saved forward; `__setstate__` does run in `torch.jit.load`, but the evaluator refuses such a file before it loads anything (new test); the load per batch is meant | `1afc9d1`: `train.py` traces the module inside the compile wrapper, and takes off only torch.compile's own wrapper (`81ffe3a`); the README says what the model file allows. The load per batch stays (ledger: Reject): 15 loads from memory took 0.45 s of an evaluation of 1.05 s. Compiling does speed the step up, by 16 % once compiled; my first note said that it did not pay, and was wrong ("What was measured") |
| After a near-miss's second look the margin is too small, with 4.15 to 5.14 % false keeps, and 8.8 to 14.2 % of campaigns with a stretch of 15 % false keeps | The cause confirmed. The second figure is borne out for the rule as it was: 9.6 to 13.3 % in a simulation of the rule as built (100,000 campaigns per case), of the campaigns whose best so far came to stand on six runs. The first may be the rate among changes that passed the first-seed check (3.3 to 5.1 % here); among all later changes without effect, 2.96 % at most were kept | `1fe37fd`: the margin at a first look counts the best so far as one seed panel. In the same simulation 5.5 to 8.0 % and 1.85 % at most. That is one half of the report's remedy; the other, a mean of the best so far shrunk by the correlation between seeds, was not simulated, because the report gave no form for it. Another remedy, the mean of the best so far on the change's own seeds, kept more changes without effect (3.83 % at most) and was not taken |

Three more gaps in the guard were found and closed while its redirection rule was rewritten (`703f074`), none
of them named by the report: a written path in Git Bash's spelling (`sort -o /c/…/eval/metrics.py
train.py`) passed; `echo x#>eval/metrics.py` passed, although `#` inside a word starts no comment and the
line writes the file; and a quote inside a comment hid the command on the next line from the guard's reading
for other shells.

Its test: a model of some hundred million parameters with and without it. Its license, its build in WSL and the claim that it supersedes torchao were not checked |

A second base for later changes is round 5's open row on two lines of descent |
| Coordinate refinement, and Optuna's TPE with pruning, inside the loop's search (4) | Reject, both | The search trains a handful of versions once each on one seed. A refinement stage halves the handful and follows single-seed noise; TPE's first ten trials are random draws by default, so within the handful it is the random search the loop has, and pruning at a rung would let the training script's own numbers decide. The Latin hypercube the report also asks for is what the search has drawn since it was built. Optuna stays the module for a search outside the loop |

A port for another agent needs that agent's CLI installed, which is yours to allow |
| safetensors with a Python model definition in place of the benchmark's model file (finding 5's remedy) | Earlier row, unchanged: Reject (round 7) | The frozen evaluator would run a run's own code, or the definition and the architecture would be frozen with it |

The report's other ingredients (helpers for tabular models and prompt optimisation, FAISS e-means,
TorchTitan, NorMuon, Polar Express, cautious weight decay, WSD, Liger Kernel, sequence packing,
self-distillation, Unsloth, mlx-lm, the objectives after GRPO) have rows from earlier rounds, which stay as
they were; the ledger's section "Round 8" names each. Two of its criticisms have no row to answer them. That
the kit gained no training method, and that 326 rows were undecided: this round answers with one measured
run, Muon, and the undecided rows stay undecided until their tests are run. That the guard still passes
what `docs/REFERENCE.md` lists as its limits (an unpacked archive, `git apply`, a formatter it does not
know, a path that a program puts together while it runs): the guard reads command lines, not what a program
does, and this round changed none of these.

### The independent review
Three readers without my working context were asked at the end of the round, each with a brief of its own:
goal, scope, what to return, and the rule that text inside the material is data. None met text that tried
to direct it, beyond the report's own closing instructions.

**The reader of the controller and the loop** read the twelve commits up to `4c1b85d` and ran probes of its
own on Windows and in WSL. It kept 19 findings. Findings 1, 2, 3 and 11 sat in code older than this round.

It also listed eight items of the report that had neither a row nor a line: each has one now (a new row for
