**The reader of the guard was stopped before it reported.** Its brief asked for a review of this round's
changes to the guard. The model's safeguards stopped it: they judge what a request asks for, and a reading
that looks for ways past a guard is close to what they are built to stop. The notice said not to do the
stopped reader's work in the working session, and I did not: no search for ways past the guard was made
here, and no second reader was sent with the same request reworded. What that leaves without an independent
reading of its own: the redirection rule (`703f074`), the routine mark (`d7265c8`), the forced `git clean`
rule (`f429101`), and the guard's side of the patterns by full path and under `~` (`53838a6`, `8dcc12f`).
What these changes do have: the kit's own tests, among them the generated test that runs every line the
guard lets pass in a real shell (in the final runs
15,600 generated lines under bash, zsh and PowerShell, of which the guard let 5,257 pass and none
did harm; "Tests"), and what the reader of the claims checked in passing at
`4c1b85d`: the report's four redirection lines pass, 48 variants of a write to a frozen file are refused,
the sealed folder outside the project is refused under both spellings, and the routine mark was too wide
(its finding 7, fixed). The reader of the controller and the loop did not read the guard's file. A second
reading by another session or model is in "What needs your decision"; Anthropic describes a verification
programme for security work that its safeguards stop
(support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-real-time-cyber-safeguards-on-claude).

### What was measured
All on 15 November 2026, on this machine.
- **Optimizers on the kit's benchmark** (`benchmarks/charlm`: a character model of 1.8M parameters, runs of
  30 s on one RTX 5090 in WSL, PyTorch 2.9.1, seeds 11 to 13, scores on `data/loopval.txt` in nats per
  character, lower is better; rates chosen on `data/dev.txt`):

  | Arm | Loss (sd) | Steps in 30 s |
  |---|---|---|
  | The shipped script: AdamW, 3e-4, constant | 1.6886 (0.0070) | |
  | AdamW, 1e-3, 100 warm-up steps, linear decay | 1.6748 (0.0102) | about 5,000 |
  | Muon (rate 0.02, no weight decay, the original rate adjustment) for the 2-D weights inside the blocks, AdamW at 1e-3 for the rest, same schedule | 1.6483 (0.0077) | about 2,720 |

  The difference between the last two is 0.0265: a t of 3.6 with about 4 degrees of freedom, one-sided p
  near 0.01. A repeat of both arms at seed 11 gave 1.6762 and 1.6498, which moved Muon's score by 0.010,
  more than its spread across seeds, and AdamW's by 0.003; with the repeats in place of the first runs the
  difference is 0.024. AdamW stopped at about Muon's number of steps scored 1.6942, so Muon's edge is not
  bought with steps. Both peak rates were bracketed on one development seed, seven settings per family.
  **Limits:** one small task, one machine, three seeds; both development curves were flat at the end, and
  no longer run was made; the AdamW rate beside Muon stayed at 1e-3 in all seven settings and was not tuned;
  the AdamW arm with matched update size, which the literature asks for, was not run; weight decay was not
  tuned. The trials that the two ledger rows had named (a model of 10M to 30M parameters for five minutes;
  ten-minute runs) were not run as written: the benchmark's 0.9 MB of text is built for runs of 30 s, and a
  larger model or a longer run on it would mostly measure overfitting. That is expected, not measured.
  These losses are on the loop's validation split, not on the test split, and do not compare with the
  pilot's numbers in point 1 of "Read this first". The benchmark's shipped `train.py` keeps AdamW on
  purpose: it is the task's starting point for an agent.
- **False keeps after a near-miss** (the sixth finding): campaigns of 34 runs, three seeds, normal noise,
  the seed carrying 0, 0.3 or 0.5 of the variance, 100,000 campaigns per case, ideas without effect. A later
  change was kept in 2.96, 2.35 and 2.14 % of cases before the change and in 1.85, 1.36 and 1.22 % after
  it. Among the changes that had passed the first-seed check, the rate was 5.09, 3.80 and 3.34 % for the
  rule as it was. In 22, 17 and 12 % of campaigns the best so far came to stand on six runs; of these, the
  share that then kept 15 % or more of the changes judged against it fell from 13.3 to 8.0 %, from 10.4 to
  6.0 % and from 9.6 to 5.5 %. Not simulated: noise that is not normal, a change that alters the noise, a
  campaign with restarts, and the report's shrunk mean of the best so far.
- **The seed × item formula** (pillar 3). My first simulation (three seeds, 400 items, 1,500 pairs of
  changes per case, four noise settings) found the formula 13 to 18 % above the true standard error, where
  the estimate from seed means was within 2 %, and I rejected the formula on that. The reader of the claims
  showed that the excess came from my simulation's clamp at zero. Without the clamp the formula is 0.98 to
  1.03 times the truth in my rerun, and 1.25 times where the effect differs by item. In the reader's own
  simulation (seed share 1, 14, 50 and 94 %) the formula with a multiplier of 2 kept 73 to 82 % of effects
  of 3 standard errors, where seed means with a t of 4 degrees of freedom kept 56 to 61 %; it kept 1.3 to
  2.5 % of changes without effect where the seed carries 1 or 14 % of the variance, and 4.0 and 9.5 % where
  it carries 50 and 94 %. So it has more power, and too many false keeps where seeds dominate. Not run: the
  kit's own keep rule with its pooled variance on the same cases, which is the row's test.
- **Compiling at the benchmark's size.** Once compiled, the training step ran at 189.0 steps a second
  against 162.4, which is 16 % more (WSL2, PyTorch 2.9.1, the step alone on a fixed batch of 64, windows of
  5 s). The first call took 1.4 s, and 4.8 s in an earlier probe; the first window after it ran at 125.6.
  For a run of 30 s that works out at about 4 % more steps, or 9 % fewer with the longer first call:
  arithmetic from these figures, not a timed run. My first note, 138.6 against 151.7 and "it did not pay",
  had timed the window that held the compiling of the backward pass.
- **The read-only sandbox** (`9e43544`), in WSL2 with bubblewrap 0.9.0: each line of the probe that had
  worked in the old box is refused in the new one, the sealed data stays hidden, CUDA works, and
  `torch.compile` builds its kernel. A campaign on the benchmark trained its three baseline runs and two
  controls on the GPU in the new box, the evaluator scored each in its own box (1.6835, 1.6821 and 1.6884;
  controls 4.1744 and 3.3103), and the self-test passed. Hugging Face `datasets` 5.2.0 in the box:
  `load_dataset` of a local file fails with the default cache and works with `HF_DATASETS_CACHE` in `/tmp`
  or in the run folder.
- **Smaller runs:** the spending cap under three launches at one moment; the frozen hash over a file of
  1 GiB (0.65 s on Windows, 0.44 s in WSL, from the file cache) and a launch with a frozen file of 65 MiB
  (0.5 s and 0.6 s); the evaluator's loads (above); the process count inside the sandbox (205, then 2); the
  guard's answers to the report's lines and to seven edits whose text names a sealed path.

### Changes in the behaviour of existing features
**The guard asks less in one case (`703f074`).** A line whose only write is a redirection (`>`, `>>`, `2>`
and the like) or a `tee` at the start of a command is now judged by its targets: only they are matched
against the frozen and harness files, git's own files and the folders of live runs (the last two added to
this sentence on 16 November: the code matched them from the start), from every folder the line goes to.
Before, such a line was asked
about when any path on it was such a file, so `python eval/metrics.py > score.json` and `cat .git/config >
gitconfig.txt` were questions, and refusals where nobody can be asked. The old rule still holds for whatever
cannot be read that way: a variable, a command's output, a backslash or a home sign in the line, a target
that is a pattern or is missing, `cd -` or `popd`, a second write verb that the guard lists, a `tee` that
starts no command, a line inside `bash -c`; and since 16 November a line with a here-document and a `cd`
or `pushd` with no folder, both of which this rule had read wrongly ("The second reading of the guard's
changes of round 8"). Reason: the loop's and a headless session's ordinary evaluation lines stopped at the
question. Tests: cases in `tests/test_kit.py`, among them writes that must stay a question (`echo x >
eval/metrics.py`, `cat gitconfig.txt > .git/config`, a target behind a variable or `cd`), and the generated
test.

**The guard asks more in five cases, each allowed before.** From `703f074`: a written word that the guard
cannot place inside the project (Git Bash's `/c/Users/…`, a mounted drive) is searched for a kept file's
name, as the whole line was, which also catches an output option with such a path; `echo
x#>eval/metrics.py`; and a command on the line after a comment that holds a quote, in the guard's reading
for other shells. Reason: each wrote a frozen file without a question. From `f429101`: `git clean -d -f`
and `git clean --force`, because the rule read a forced clean only with its `-f` in the first group of
letters. A clean that only lists (`-n`, `--dry-run`) passes as before. Tests: cases in `tests/test_kit.py`
and `tests/test_review_fixes.py`.

**The guard's reasons and record, with no answer changed (`d7265c8`, `f429101`).** A formatter that is given
a folder with kept files has a reason of its own ("A formatter would rewrite files that this guard keeps
…"; it shared the whole-folder reason). A forced push carries the push's reason beside the destructive one.
A forced `git clean` that names a frozen or harness file, or a folder that holds one, carries that reason
beside the destructive one, so its question shows two reasons. The guard's record of a refusal carries
`"routine": true` when its every reason is a git undo or the formatter's reason; a refusal with any other
reason beside them is not routine. Tests: `tests/test_kit.py`, `tests/test_loop.py`,
`tests/test_review_fixes.py`.

**Patterns by full path or under `~` (`53838a6`, `8dcc12f`).** The guard takes `sealed_paths`,
`frozen_paths` and `harness_paths` from `expctl.load_config`, which now gives them in one form: `~` written
out, and a full path that leads into the project as the name it has there. So for such a pattern the guard
receives the name in the project, as for a pattern written that way. What the guard answered for the full
spelling before was not examined beyond the reviewer's note that it refused the file itself. The guard's
own fallback reading of the config file, for when `expctl` cannot be imported, is unchanged. Tests:
`tests/test_kit.py` (with a `~` pattern and with a full path into the project the guard refuses the read,
and `expctl selftest` asks it about the place itself), `tests/test_loop.py`.

**A limit of the guard that is now written down, unchanged.** A line that removes a folder in which sealed
files lie, and no frozen or harness file (`rm -rf data` with `data/test/**` sealed), is not asked about:
the files are deleted, not read. A move, a rename or a recursive copy of such a folder is asked about. The
reader of the claims pointed this out; it was so before the round. `docs/REFERENCE.md` lists it.

**A new harness path (`6cd4ee3`).** `.claude/state/frozen-hashes.json`, where `expctl` keeps the hashes of
large frozen files, joins `harness_paths` in the defaults and in the kit's config, so the guard asks before
an agent writes it. On an upgrade the installer's existing step adds the path to a project's config and
names it; that is this round's one migration. Test: the guard's answer to a Write and to a shell one-liner
in `tests/test_kit.py`; the upgrade in `tests/test_ports.py`.

**The loop.**
- A routine refusal does not void an iteration; it still counts in `guard_denials`. Every other refusal
  voids it as before: an undo or a formatter aimed at a frozen file, a forced `git clean` aimed at a kept
  file or folder, a push, a stopped run, a read of sealed data, a line whose other command the guard
  refuses too. A change voided only by its session's refused calls is no longer remembered as tried, so a
  later session may propose it again. A refused call that itself names a sealed path or token still bars
  its change for the campaign, because the tamper scan reads a session's calls whatever the guard answered
  (`d7265c8`, `f429101`).
- The margin announced after a second look is larger: the root of 1.0 where it was the root of 0.75. The
  second look itself is unchanged (`1fe37fd`). A resumed campaign shows this version's margin, so it may
  show another figure than its last session saw; no verdict changes, since every decision works the margin
  out anew (`27f318f`).
- A campaign whose `loop.seeds` names a seed twice no longer starts or resumes (`27f318f`).
- A protected file of more than 64 MiB is hashed in full once in a campaign's process, and again when its
  size, its times or its first or last MiB differ; before every keep and every confirmation's verdict all
  are read in full (`6cd4ee3`). On Windows, where a file has no change time, they are also read in full
  after every evaluation: one read of each such file per run, 0.65 s for 1 GiB from the file cache
  (`e334c3a`). What remains on Windows: nothing confines a run's processes there, so one that a run left
  behind could still undo a change between the evaluator's read and that check.
- A training run and the evaluator in the bubblewrap sandbox get a process namespace where the system
  accepts it (`c858226`), and **the file system read-only** (`9e43544`): a training run writes its
  worktree and its own run folder, the evaluator the folder it scores and `loop.eval_writable`; `/tmp`,
  `/run` and `/dev/shm` are the box's own. **A training script or an evaluator that writes anywhere else
  now fails with "Read-only file system"**, and data, an interpreter or a socket under the system's `/tmp`
  is not seen. The loop's message for such a failure names the places a run may write, and
  `references/loop.md` has a paragraph "What a sandboxed run can write". Not closed: a socket file under
  the home folder stays reachable, a run reads whatever the account can read apart from the sealed paths,
  and of a second mount of the same disk only WSL's `/mnt/wslg` is hidden. Linux with bubblewrap only;
  Windows and macOS have no sandbox of the loop, as before.
- The loop takes a run as ended when the supervisor that its own launch started has gone, not when a file
  in the run's folder says so, and counts a run's GPU time itself, from the launch to the end. Its
  GPU-hours now include runs that were stopped or cut off (`25f5a24`).
- The tamper scan. Where a run has no process namespace, a change that adds `os.kill` or `os.killpg`
  counts as tampering: a scan, not a wall (`c858226`). Where a run has no sandbox, a comment line of a
  Python file is no longer read as code, so the comment "no subprocess here" no longer voids a change; a
  comment after code, a string, and a comment in a file that is not Python count as before, and so does a
  sealed token or path in any comment. An added line that begins with `++` is now read (`27f318f`).
- The worker's prompt has history lines for the last five changes that were not kept, with the note that
  these are the training script's numbers, not the evaluator's score. Series names and steps come from
  training code and are cleaned as the best run's curve was: plain ASCII characters, numbers only
  (`1933688`).

**The controller.**
- `frozen_hash` changes once for a project with frozen files beyond 64 MB (`6cd4ee3`). `expctl status`
  takes the older hash of a ranked run for the same files, so runs made before the change raise no alert.
- `expctl launch` and `nnremote launch` read every frozen file, as `expctl hash` and the final evaluation
  did; the hash in a run's record depends on no file in the project (`e451124`). Cost: 0.65 s for 1 GiB
  from the file cache, and as long as the disk needs for a first read. The kept hashes serve `expctl
  status` alone: a hash written there, or a large file changed with its times set back, can make `status`
  miss a change until the next launch, `expctl hash` or final evaluation.
- `expctl stop` on Linux signals only a process that `/proc` shows was started for the run: the supervisor
  by the run's folder in its command line, a launched command by `EXP_RUN_DIR` in its environment, a
  script that was run directly by the run's metrics file held open for writing. Where nothing is proven,
  nothing is signalled, the output says so, and the exit code is 1. The supervisor now acts on a
  `stop.json` in its run's folder on every system, whatever time the request names (it did so on Windows
  only, and only for a request newer than the launch), so a run whose records prove nothing is stopped all
  the same. A run past its deadline and grace is killed after the `kill_after_s` of its launch, whatever a
  request file says. macOS and Windows have no `/proc`: which process a stop signals is unchanged there
  (`25f5a24`).
- A launched command may hold `{run_dir}`, which the supervisor replaces by the run's folder; the manifest
  keeps the placeholder, so `expctl resume` binds the new run's folder (`9e43544`).
- `load_run` no longer takes a heartbeat's process number for a run whose command has `--unshare-pid`: a
  boxed run that ended without a record is "lost" at once. `shortcut:` only bubblewrap's flag is
  recognised (`c858226`).
- A sealed, frozen or harness pattern given by full path or under `~` names one place for expctl, nnloop,
  nnremote, the session-start hook and the guard (`8dcc12f`). Before, a folder of the project sealed by
  its full path stayed in a snapshot, a campaign's worktree and a remote run's archive. A snapshot now
  judges the place a git-ignored link leads to by the patterns that are full paths. The session-start
  hook's line and the name of `selftest`'s sealed check show a `~` pattern written out. **A campaign begun
  under a pattern that names a folder of the project by its full path stops at its next check after the
  upgrade with "protected file(s) changed": start it anew.** Left as written: `loop.protected_data`, and
  the config that a remote run's archive carries.

**Remote runs.**
- Ledger rows are written with LF on Windows too, and every ledger write on Linux and macOS waits for the
  file lock. Where no lock is to be had, a launch that does not find its own row refuses and books a settle
  row of $0 (`6450d1c`).
- A job that outlasted its reserved time has used it up, by the larger of the clock's count and the
  controller's own. Before, with the clock set back during a run, a job that the provider had ended at its
  time limit was resumed as a new job with a reservation of its own (`1787de0`).
- A price, hours or a cap that is no finite number above zero reserves nothing; `--hours nan` and `--hours
  inf` are refused, for a free target too. A ledger row with such an amount, or one below zero, counts as a
  damaged ledger and refuses every paid start until it is repaired. **A cap of Infinity is no cap any
  more: it reads "no spending cap is set".** Every failure between a reservation and the controller's start
  books the $0 settlement (`1599a6b`).

**The benchmark (`1afc9d1`, `81ffe3a`).** `benchmarks/charlm/train.py` saves the module inside
torch.compile's wrapper when the model was compiled, and any other model whole.

**Existing tests that changed:**
- `tests/test_kit.py`: `cat .git/config > gitconfig.txt` expected a question and expects none (`703f074`).
- `tests/test_loop.py`: the Codex campaign in the guard tests now carries a refused `git restore train.py`
  and expects `guard_denials == 1` with the iteration decided on its score; `tests/fake_agent.py` gained the
  step `sh COMMAND`, which is shown to the guard and never run (`d7265c8`).
- `tests/test_loop.py`: `second_panel` expected the smaller margin in two places and expects the larger one
  (`1fe37fd`).
- `tests/test_remote.py`: the cap-race test is rewritten, because its rival wrote through the function that
  now holds the lock. The rival is a writer without a lock whose row lands behind the launch's read or
  behind its write, with a third case in which the launch's own row is missing (`6450d1c`).
- `tests/test_ports.py`: the upgrade test expects the new harness path among those an upgrade adds
  (`6cd4ee3`).
- `tests/test_loop.py`, the sandbox checks: the probe lies in the project and the folder with sealed data
  outside the project under `/var/tmp`, because a box has a `/tmp` of its own; and the runs folder is
  expected not to be writable for a training run, because the behaviour changed (`9e43544`).
- `tests/test_kit.py`: the check of a hash written into the kept file asserted that a launch's call takes
  it; it asserts that the call a launch makes gives the true hash and that only the call `status` makes
  takes the written one (`e451124`).
- `tests/test_loop.py`: the check of sealed data outside the project asks the evaluator's box about four
  pairs of pattern and command where it asked about one, and the check of a folder hidden as one compares
  the mount point by its real path (`8dcc12f`).
- `tests/test_loop.py`: the unit check of large protected files also asks the check that follows an
  evaluation (`e334c3a`).
- `tests/test_benchmarks.py`: two checks of `1afc9d1` printed their premise and passed either way; both
  assert it now (`81ffe3a`).
- `tests/test_loop.py`: the routine mark's table of lines gains a forced clean of the project and an undo
  with a harmless second command (both routine) and a forced clean of a frozen folder and of a frozen file
  (neither routine) (`f429101`).

  answers to the report's lines; the cap race; the frozen hash over a large file; the benchmark's saves and
  the evaluator's refusal of a file whose module writes while it loads; the simulations; the optimizer

- **Unverified:** everything new on macOS and on bare Linux, the read-only sandbox and the proofs behind a

  under PyTorch 2.15; the report's version pins for its packs; Chronos-2's release and license; Transformer
  Engine's license and build; whether the history lines change what campaigns reach; the ledger's lock

  tests cover the parts).

### Things to know
- **The guard's changes of this round have had no independent reading of their own** ("The independent
  review"). They are the part of this round I would have read again first. (Read on 16 November: two
  regressions found and fixed, "The second reading of the guard's changes of round 8".)
- **A comment that names a sealed path is still a question.** An edit that adds `# reminder: never read
  data/test` to `train.py` is asked about, and refused where nobody can be asked; in a campaign it also
  bars its change, whatever the guard answered. The guard does not parse the languages of the files it
  reads, and `sed -i 's/^# //' train.py` turns a comment into code without naming a path, so the edit is
  the one moment at which the path can be seen. A note in a Markdown file that names the path passes, and
  so does a comment that says "the test split".
- **A training script that writes outside its worktree and its run folder fails in the loop's sandbox on
  Linux** since `9e43544`. A cache belongs in the box's `/tmp` or in the run folder.
- **The kit's references now hold a result measured on the pilot's own task.** A later pilot's kit arm
  starts with knowledge of the task that the other arms lack. `docs/REFERENCE.md` says so where it
  describes the pilot; a fair pilot now needs another task.
- **Three commit messages of this round say something that a later commit corrects**, and a message cannot
  change: `1afc9d1` ("compiling did not pay"; corrected by `dc4fcd6`), `6cd4ee3` (that a file's change time
  gives a planted change away on Linux and macOS, and that the loop catches such a change before a keep;
  corrected by `e451124` and `e334c3a`), and `53838a6` ("seven calls": six refused calls and one control).
- **Two faults of my own in the guard's new redirection rule** failed checks of the kit's tests at their
  first run and were fixed before the commit (`703f074`).
- **With the temporary folder behind a link, ten checks of `tests/test_loop.py` failed in WSL** when I
  tried it at `2947666`, and `tests/test_kit.py` passed there (898 checks). Not run again after the review's
  fixes, which changed the sandbox and the way a pattern reaches it. The cause was in the
  tests: they build a campaign from a project path that still has the link in it, which the kit's own start
  never does, and bubblewrap refuses a mount point behind a link. A bind that fails makes a run fail at its
  start; it does not run unconfined. On macOS, where the temporary folder is such a link, there is no
  bubblewrap and those checks are skipped.
- **One removal was refused.** A command of mine that would have removed a temporary folder under the WSL
  home was refused by this environment's safety check. I did not work around it; my probes have cleaned up
  through Python's temporary folders since. Left behind in the WSL home: `~/nn-kit-probe/` (about 1.5 GB,
  from round 7), `~/nnkit-upgrade/` with the test environments, `~/nnkit-r5fix/`, `~/nnkit-tmp/` and two
  `~/tmp*` folders; an Alpine image in WSL's Docker; and `nnkit-upgrade` in the Windows temporary folder.
- **Cut for the usage limit:** no further optimizer arms (the matched-update control, weight decay, a
  second task); the test of the seed × item formula with the kit's own keep rule; no environments built
  for the report's packs; no agent sessions; a second attempt at a reading of the guard's changes; the
  round's probe and simulation scripts are not in the repository (this section records their settings).

## The second reading of the guard's changes of round 8 (16 November 2026): two regressions found and fixed

(Added with "The reading of the fixes", further down: the fixes of this section have been read since. That
reading corrects what is marked here as added with it, and it found one more regression of round 8.)

With round 8 on its test branch I asked whether `main` should take it, and you answered "Second reading
first". This section is that reading and what followed from it. Its commits are `332fd85` (the guard and
its tests, and the two pages of the kit that describe the rules) and the commit of this record. Both were
local when this section was written, and `main` was unchanged. On your "Push test branch" of the same day
they went to the test branch, where all six of GitHub's jobs pass on them: "The fixes of the second
reading on the test branch", the section after this one. Where this section says that nothing is pushed,
or that GitHub's machines and a Mac have not run these commits, that section is the later word.

### In short

1. **The guard's three changes of round 8 have now been read by someone other than their author.** I started
   one fresh agent with no access to this session, on another model (Opus 5.5), with read access only. Its
   question was whether each changed rule does what its comment, its tests and my description say, and which
   branches have no test. It was not asked for ways past the guard: the brief that the model's safeguards
   stopped on 15 November was not repeated. It was not stopped, and it changed nothing.
2. **It found two regressions in the round's one change that makes the guard ask less** (`703f074`, the
   targets of a redirection). An apostrophe in a here-document paired with a quote further down the line and
   hid a redirection to a frozen file between them; and a `cd` or `pushd` with no folder, which goes home or
   to the folder before, was read as if the line stayed where it was. In both cases a line that writes a
   frozen file passed unasked, and had been asked about before round 8. **Both are fixed.**
3. **One gap of the same cause is older than round 8, and is fixed too.** The reader noted in passing that a
   write verb in that place (`cp x.py eval/metrics.py` behind a here-document's apostrophe) passed in both
   versions. I ran it: so it was, also with a quoted or indented closing word and with PowerShell's
   here-string. The guard now reads every line once more with the quote characters taken out of its
   here-documents. Sealed data was not affected: the same line with a read of sealed data was refused before
   and is refused now.
4. **A forced `git clean` that takes ignored files along is no longer a routine refusal.** `git clean -fdx`
   with no path was marked routine for the unattended loop, although `-x` deletes what git ignores, where
   data, run folders and checkpoints usually lie; the same command with a path was not. It now carries a
   second reason. `git clean -fd` keeps the mark.
5. **Three findings are answered without a change to what the guard asks**, each with its reason below: an
   archive unpacked over a frozen file, a forced clean recognised across a line break, and a second pass
   over lines that hold a comment. Two descriptions of mine were narrower or wider than the code and are
   corrected.
6. **The fixes cost questions, and I chose that.** A line with a here-document is judged as it was before
   round 8: if it writes anything, and the redirection that saves the document counts, and it names a kept
   file anywhere, the document's text included, it is asked about. So a note that a here-document writes,
   and whose text names the evaluator's file, is a question again, and a refusal where nobody can be asked;
   it passed between `703f074` and this fix. The line that round 8 was after still passes
   (`python eval/metrics.py > score.json`). Every change of this section makes the guard ask or refuse
   more; none makes it ask less. (Added with "The reading of the fixes": this left out a cost. The extra
   reading also refused harmless programs to a read-only subagent, until the fix of that section.)
7. **Tests.** All eight test files pass on the commit of the fix under six interpreters:
   1,572, 1,559 and 1,560 checks in WSL and 1,557, 1,544 and 1,545 on Windows. That is 13 more in every
   run than before: the 13 new lines of the guard's table.
8. **Still open.** The fixes are mine, and no independent reader has read them. GitHub's machines have not run
   these commits, so they have not run on a Mac. The reader's own list of what it did not check stands below.

### The findings, one by one

The reader compared the guard before the round (`3d7a4a7`) with the guard after it (`47f07a6`) by calling
both on the same lines, with one frozen folder and no live run. It executed none of the lines and did not
run the test files. "Certain" and "low" are its own words.

What it confirmed, by commit. `703f074`: every spelling of a redirection that the rule reads (`>`, `>>`,

command's start, targets read from every folder the line goes to, and the fall back to the older rule for a
variable, a backtick, a backslash, a home sign, a pattern, a nested shell and a second listed verb.
`d7265c8`: the mark is set only where the answer is an ask and every reason is a routine one, before an ask
becomes a refusal; a forced push carries both reasons. `f429101`: the `-f` is found in any group of options

### Changes in the behaviour of existing features

The guard, each asking or refusing more than before. The tests are in the guard's table of
`tests/test_kit.py` for the first three and in the routine mark's check of `tests/test_loop.py` for the
fourth.

- **A line with a here-document** (`<<WORD`, not the here-string `<<<`) is not read target by target. The
  rule from before round 8 decides: when the line writes anything, every path on it counts as written.
  Reason: finding 1. Put to the guard before the round, after it and now, six lines of this kind that write
  no kept file are asked about before and now, and passed in between: a note by a here-document whose text
  names the frozen file (with a plain closing word, with a quoted one, and with an apostrophe in the text),
  a here-document beside an evaluator run with and without saved output, and a Python program from a
  here-document that reads the frozen file and saves what it prints. Not asked about in any of the three:
  a here-document that names no kept file, one that is only printed, a commit message from one. (Added
  with "The reading of the fixes": the last was wrong for a message that quotes a command with a kept file
  in it, `"rm eval/metrics.py"`. `332fd85` asked about that; with the fix of that section it passes again.)
- **A `cd`, `pushd`, `chdir`, `sl`, `Set-Location` or `Push-Location` with no folder, a `pushd +1` or `-1`,
  and a `cd` with only a redirection behind it** take the older rule too. Reason: finding 2.
- **One more reading of every line**, without the quote characters inside its here-documents. Any rule may
  now ask or refuse where a quote in a document's text had hidden what stands further down. That reaches
  text which no shell runs: `cat <<EOF`, then `don't; rm eval/metrics.py`, then `EOF` and `echo 'end'`
  passed before round 8 and after it and is asked about now, as the same text without the apostrophe
  always was. A `<<` inside quoted text counts as a document's start, and then the quoted texts below it
  are read as words. A closing word that starts with a digit or a sign, or is quoted in part (`<<1`,
  `<<E"O"F`), is not read as one: such a document keeps its quotes, and the gap of point 3 stays open for
  it. The reference names that limit. (Added with "The reading of the fixes": a word quoted in part is
  read now; the limit is a word that starts with a digit or a sign.) Reason: the gap noted under finding 1.
- **A forced `git clean` with `-x` or `-X`** is asked about with two reasons. Attended, nothing else
  changes. In the unattended loop its refusal makes the iteration `invalid`; it was routine since
  `d7265c8`. Reason: finding 4.

Nothing else changed: no change to the installer, to `expctl`, to the loop's code or to a file format.

   (`print('loss -> 1')` held a "redirection"), and the main session was asked about a commit message that

### What I found while fixing

None of these is the reader's. Each was found by putting lines to the guard of each version.

- **A regression of round 8 (`703f074`), on the public `main` since the push of point 22**: point 3 above.
  Six lines of this kind, and the five of finding 3, were asked about before round 8, passed in round 8
  and with the fixes of the second reading, and are asked about now. The fix has two parts. A `cd` is
  followed at more places where a command starts: behind the `)` of a `case` pattern, behind zsh's
  `noglob` and `nocorrect`, and behind a redirection that stands first. And anywhere else a `cd` with a
  word behind it (`time -p cd ..`), or one whose option the guard does not know (zsh's `cd -q data`),
  brings back the rule from before round 8 for that line: every path that it names counts as written. So
  the guard need not know every place where a shell starts a command. The cost: a line that holds the
  words `cd data` or `cd -P` as arguments, a write and a kept file is asked about, as before round 8.
- **A here-document that nothing on the line closes** passed in my first form of fix 1 with an apostrophe
  and a `cp` behind it, where `332fd85` asked. Kept strict: such a document loses all of its quote
  characters. The cost: a read-only subagent's program from a document left open is still refused.
- **My first form of fix 2** tied `popd`, `Pop-Location` and `cd -` to the places where a command starts
  and lost them behind a `case` pattern and as arguments. They count anywhere on the line, as before.
- **Left as it is, stricter than needed:** a comment with `-x` on the clean's own line
  (`git clean -fd # not -x`) still takes the routine mark away.
- **Three kinds of line take seconds to read.** A here-document with 4,000 escaped quotes on one line:
  3.8 s. One open quote in front of 4,000 backslash pairs: 6.0 s. 5,000 continued lines of
  `git clean -f`: 6.3 s. All three are older than round 8 (2.9 s, 2.9 s and 6.3 s on `3d7a4a7`); the
  extra reading of `332fd85` added 0.8 s and 3.2 s to the first two, and this fix at most 0.2 s. Of
  eleven other long lines one takes 0.7 s on every version (4,000 backslashes) and ten take 0.1 s or
  less, the new rules for `cd` among them. Not changed: the reader looked for slow paths and named none,
  and I know no way for such a line to come from an agent at work. It stays a known weakness.

## The second reading of the fixes (17 November 2026): a regression of my last fix, and three older gaps

(Added with "The second reading's fixes on the test branch", the section after this one: on your "Push test
branch" these commits went to the test branch, where five of GitHub's six jobs pass on them. That section
is the later word wherever this one says that nothing is pushed, that GitHub's machines have not run these
commits, or that the clock of WSL alone made the two checks fail.)

To the question whether the fixes get one more reading before round 8 reaches your real install, you
answered "Read again first". I took the word to cover what I had said it would: a fresh reader with read
access only goes through the fix `4e2bec4`; I check each finding by running it, fix or answer it, test,
and commit locally. Not covered: a push, your real install, deleting a branch.

In short:

1. **The fix that the public `main` holds brought a regression.** `4e2bec4` kept the quotes that pair
   inside a here-document. With a backslash in front of a quote in the document (`print("a \" b")`, or
   JSON with `"5\" screen"`) the rules paired that quote with one behind the document, and a write of a
   frozen file between the two passed without a question. The commit before it, `332fd85`, asked. The
   reader found it in the guard's helpers; I confirmed it on the whole guard. Fixed in `63bfdf6`.
2. **Three older gaps of the same kind, in every version put to them, back to the one before round 8.**
   I found them while checking that fix, by putting its sibling lines to the guard: the same escaped
   quote in a quoted text with no here-document (`echo "a \" b"; cp train.py eval/metrics.py; echo
   "end"`); on PowerShell an escaped quote inside a string (``echo "a `" b"; cp ...``); and on
   PowerShell a quote inside a comment (`<# it's #> cp train.py eval/metrics.py; echo 'x'`). Each let a
   write of a frozen file pass. Fixed in `63bfdf6` (the first) and `25aa674` (the two of PowerShell).
   My fix of PowerShell's escaped quote was incomplete at first: below a comment line that holds an
   apostrophe (`# don't`), `25aa674` still let the write pass. I found that when I re-read the commit,
   and completed it in `5dcd2ec`.
3. **One more of the kind is found and left, as a named limit**: text handed to `cmd /c`. An apostrophe
   quotes nothing in cmd, so two apostrophes hide what stands between them from the rules. The reference
   names the limit, and the ledger holds the reading that would close it as adopted and unfinished.
4. **The root is one**: an escape character in front of a quote. The rules pair quotes with no escape in
   effect, and each shell has one. The guard now reads every line once more as a POSIX shell pairs its
   quotes and once more as PowerShell does. A reading only adds questions: the line as it came is still
   read as before, so no answer got weaker (by construction, and on the lines put to the guards).
   (Added on 18 November: that did not hold. Two of the new readings had taken the place of older
   ones, and two kinds of line that only the older ones asked about passed; "The reading of the three
   guard fixes".)
5. **Three costs, all on the strict side.** A read-only subagent is refused again a here-document that
   holds an escaped quote and a quoted `->` or `rm` (as before `4e2bec4`). And behind a command in
   backticks right before a closing quote (``"`date`"``), text quoted on the same line is read as
   commands: the main session is asked about a commit message there that quotes a command, and a
   read-only subagent is refused a quoted `->`. With `$( )` in place of the backticks nothing changes.
   A fourth may arise and showed on none of the lines put to the guard: PowerShell's reading takes
   every `#` outside a quoted text for a comment, inside a word too, which adds a question where a
   quoted text opens behind such a `#` and closes on a later line.
6. **The reader's five other points are answered**: one is on the strict side and known, one (speed)
   did not show in my timing, one is meant and is now described exactly, one got its test rows, and one
   was three sentences of the reference and a comment. (Added on 18 November: the fixes written on
   this reading brought three slow kinds of line of their own, which that timing did not try; "The
   reading of the three guard fixes".)
7. **Tests.** On the final commit, `5dcd2ec`: Windows, all pass under three interpreters (1,624, 1,611

### What I found while fixing

None of these is the reader's. Each was found by putting lines to the guard of each version: the one
before round 8, round 8's, `332fd85`, `4e2bec4` and, for PowerShell's and cmd's, `63bfdf6`.

- **An escaped quote in a quoted text, with no here-document** (a POSIX shell). `echo "a \" b"; cp
  train.py eval/metrics.py; echo "end"` passed on every version: an odd number of `\"` inside double
  quotes shifts the pairs that the rules see. The reading of a POSIX shell now writes an escaped quote
  as the shell's own splice (`"a "'"'" b"`), which every pairing reads alike. In `63bfdf6`; four rows.
- **PowerShell's escape character** is the backtick: `` `" `` is a quote that ends nothing, inside a
  string too, and a quote inside `<# #>` belongs to the comment. Both lines of point 2 passed on every
  version, with a line comment or a here-string beside them too. The guard now reads every line once
  more as PowerShell pairs its quotes: its quoted texts, its comment and its escape are one pattern, a
  comment becomes a blank and an escaped quote is taken out. In `25aa674`; eleven rows, one check.
- **What `25aa674` missed.** Re-reading that commit against its own comment, I saw that it paired
  PowerShell's quotes first and looked for the comments to the line end afterwards, with the stripper
  of a POSIX shell. So a comment line that holds an apostrophe above the escaped quote still hid the
  write: `# don't`, and below it ``echo "a `" b"; cp train.py eval/metrics.py; echo "end" 'x'``,
  passed on `25aa674` as on every version before. And a comment behind a text that ends in a backslash
  (`"C:\out\" # don't`) was not found as one; that line was asked about, but by the POSIX reading
  alone. One more reading now takes PowerShell's quoted texts, both kinds of comment and the escape in
  one pass. The reading with the POSIX stripper stays, because a `#` inside a word starts no comment
  there, as in PowerShell's arguments. In `5dcd2ec`; four rows.
- **Why every line, and not only the PowerShell tool's**: a POSIX line may hand text to PowerShell, and
  Codex and Cursor do not say which shell runs a line. The cost with the backticks comes from that; the
  ledger holds the narrower form as rejected, with this reason.
- **cmd, left.** `cmd /c "echo it's & copy train.py eval\metrics.py & echo don't"` passes on every
  version and now; without the apostrophes it is asked about. Read so for every line, apostrophes as
  plain characters would ask about every quoted write verb, so that reading belongs where the guard
  hands text to `cmd /c`. I did not open that part under the usage limit. The reference names the limit.
- **Seen and left**, both false alarms on the strict side and both in every version: on PowerShell a
  commit message with an escaped quote in front of a command name (``git commit -m "fix `"rm`" of
  eval/metrics.py"``) is asked about, and a read-only subagent is refused `echo "5\" screen"; ls; echo
  "end"`.

### Every change in what the guard asks, refuses or allows

- **Asked about now**, each because the shell runs the write: a write of a kept file behind a
  here-document that holds an escaped quote (passed since `4e2bec4`); behind a quoted text with an
  escaped quote; on PowerShell behind a string with `` `" `` in it, or behind a comment `<# #>` with a
  quote in it (these three passed in every version); and on PowerShell below a comment line that holds
  an apostrophe, where an escaped quote follows (it passed in every version, `25aa674` included).
  Tests: ten rows of the guard's table in `tests/test_kit.py`.
- **Refused to a read-only subagent now** (two costs): a here-document with an escaped quote and a quoted
  `->` or `rm` in it (it passed since `4e2bec4` only); a quoted `->` behind a command in backticks right
  before a closing quote. The readings that close the gaps cannot tell these from the lines they are
  for. Tests: two checks in `tests/test_ports.py`.
- **Asked of the main session now** (the third cost): a commit message that quotes a command, behind a
  command in backticks right before a closing quote. Test: one row, and one for `$( )`, which passes.
- **A cost that may arise, seen on no line put to the guard**: PowerShell's reading takes every `#`
  outside a quoted text for the start of a comment, inside a word too (`${#a[@]}`). Where a quoted text
  opens behind such a `#` and closes on a later line, that adds a question, or a refusal of a read-only
  subagent. The reference names it. Test: one row with `${#a[@]}` in it, which passes.
- **The routine mark** of the loop's own lines: unchanged. Its check has four more lines: a `git clean`
  continued by `^`, or by a backtick or `^` in front of a Windows line end, loses the mark as before; a
  backslash in front of a Windows line end continues a line in no shell and leaves the mark.
- **Not weaker**: no line that was asked about or refused passes now. By construction: each new reading
  is checked in addition to the line as it came. By running: `63bfdf6` against `4e2bec4` on 130 lines
  (four answers differ), `25aa674` against `63bfdf6` on 158 (eight differ) and `5dcd2ec` against
  `25aa674` on 167 (one differs); each of the thirteen went from a pass to a question or a refusal:
  ten writes of a frozen file, and the three costs. (Added on 18 November: "by construction" was wrong
  for the two readings that had taken the place of older ones, and the lines put to the guards did not
  hold the two kinds that passed; "The reading of the three guard fixes".)
- **Limits that stay**, each named in the reference: text handed to `cmd /c`; the closing words of a
  here-document that are not read (`<<$EOF`, `<<.end`); the force flag of `git clean` read past a line
  break, which is strict.

   count said "not yet", and the stop was put down to a hang. That takes a kill that returns within
   0.05 s, which a POSIX kill does and `taskkill` on Windows does not, and a rounding that goes down,
   which is chance: so Windows never showed it, and Linux and macOS showed it once in the runs so far.
   What it costs a user: a campaign that reaches its wall-clock limit during a session can end with
   the wrong reason and exit code 1, and the confirmation of a kept change on fresh seeds, which runs
   when a campaign ends for a limit, does not run at such a stop: it waits for a resume. Nothing runs

   it back to internet time about 0.2 s later, a step of -9.1 s. And WSL's clocks tick 10 % fast,
   because the tick length of its kernel stands at 11,000 µs where 10,000 is the norm: 60 s asked of
   `sleep` took 54.6 s on a stopwatch in Windows. So a time of day read in WSL is 8.6 s ahead for
   0.2 s of every 5.5 s, and what I reported as "the clock set back 149 s within 1,644 s" is the net
   of those steps against a clock that runs fast. This explains the checks that failed there at

### The failed check, and its cause

The check resumes a campaign with a wall-clock limit seven seconds ahead and an agent that does not
answer for a minute; the test project ends a session that hangs after ten seconds. Expected: the limit
ends the session, and the campaign stops with "limit reached: hours" and exit code 0.

The job's log has the stop reason "the agent session hung: no result within 5.47706 s, so it was ended".
5.477 s is what was left of the limit when the session began, so the session was ended at the limit.
In the loop of `36a4857`, `session()` then saved the counters, which rounds the time used to 0.1 s, and
called `check()`, which measured again from the rounded count. Where the rounding had gone down, the
limit was "not reached" by up to 0.05 s, and the next line called the stop a hang.

Shown without a Mac: the new check (below) sets the loop's clocks by hand so that the session is ended
0.02 s after the limit and the count rounds down. The loop of `36a4857` answers "the agent session
hung" there.

### What WSL's clock does on this machine

Measured on 17 November 2026, each by running it, with nothing changed on the machine (WSL 2.7.11,
kernel 6.18.33, clock source `tsc`):

- `time.sleep(60)` in WSL took 54.6 s on a stopwatch in Windows; WSL's monotonic clock counted 60.0 s
  for it and its wall clock 54.5 s. Over 180 s of the monotonic clock the stopwatch counted 163.8 s.
  So WSL's monotonic clock runs 10 % fast, and its wall clock does too between two steps.
- Why it runs fast, read from the kernel without changing it (`adjtimex` with no mode set): the tick
  length is 11,000 µs, the most the kernel allows, where 10,000 is the norm. The raw clock, which
  that setting does not touch, counted 18.19 s for a sleep of 20 s, as the Windows stopwatch did. I
  do not know what set it: nothing in the kit calls `adjtimex`, and no test runs with the right to.
- Sampled every 20 ms for 180 s, the wall clock was stepped 31 times forward and 31 times back against
  the monotonic clock: about every 5.5 s (5 s of true time) a step of +8.6 s, and 0.15 to 0.4 s later
  a step of -9.1 s; once the step back came 15 s late. The net was -16.5 s: the 9 % that I had measured
  on the days before as "the clock set back". A second sample of twelve pairs, an hour later: +8.7 s,
  and -9.2 s after 0.14 to 0.26 s.
- The Windows clock was 9.1 s ahead of an internet time server (`w32tm`, against time.windows.com), and
  the Windows time service was not running when I looked (stopped, start type Manual). WSL's time
  service (`systemd-timesyncd`, against Ubuntu's server) reported an offset of -9.1 s and 20,003
  packets. So the steps are two services at odds: Hyper-V's time sync sets WSL's clock to the
  Windows time, and WSL's own service sets it back to internet time, every 5 s.
- Ubuntu's documentation for WSL describes this setup: WSL's kernel is always started with
  `hv_utils.timesync_implicit=1` (it is, here), under which each time sample from Hyper-V sets the
  guest's clock; Ubuntu 24.04 and earlier (this one is 24.04) have `systemd-timesyncd` enabled, as it
  is here; and it advises disabling that unit "to avoid conflicts with the Hyper-V implicit time
  synchronization". It says nothing of a tick length.

What it explains, each a check that failed in WSL in some runs and passed in others:

- **The loop's two wall-clock checks.** The loop counted on the wall clock alone. A count that began or
  ended inside a step forward was off by about nine seconds: a limit seven seconds ahead then seemed
  sixteen ahead, so the hang's ten seconds came first ("no result within 10 s", in all six logs); and
  a limit of 0.036 s was not reached in a whole campaign.
- **"a job the provider ends at its time limit is not resumed"** (`tests/test_remote.py`), in 8 of the
  29 WSL logs kept since 15 November. The stand-in for the provider ended a job when the wall clock
  had passed the job's limit, and asked five times a second: where it met a step forward in the job's
  first second or two, the job was killed, and the controller found it ended 1.4 to 3.1 s after its
  start, where its limit is 5 s. The controller then did what it should with a job that ends before
  its reserved time is used up: it took the job for taken away from outside and resumed it. The fault
  was the stand-in's (point 7). Shown apart from the tests: of 40 limits of 5 s, polled five times a
  second in WSL, 25 ended early on the wall clock, 9 of them within 1.5 s, and none on the monotonic
  clock. The remote tests themselves, run four times with each stand-in, passed all eight times: at
  one failure in four runs that shows nothing either way.
- **"a run past its deadline is killed after kill_after_s ..."** (`tests/test_kit.py`), in two WSL logs
  of 16 November and once on 17 November, each time "stopped for None". The check gives a run a
  deadline two seconds ahead, and a run compares its deadline with the wall clock (`runlog.py`). Read
  inside a step forward the deadline has passed, and the run ends by itself before the test's part
  begins: "after 8.9 s" is the step and a third of a second. That is read from the code and the
  numbers; no rerun shows it. A real deadline lies hours ahead and loses nine seconds. Left as it is.
- **"session hook injects status after compaction"** (`tests/test_kit.py`), on 17 November, and once on

  older or younger than it is, and the test project calls a run stalled after 3 s. A project's own
  setting is 900 s unless it is changed, which no such step reaches. Left as it is: the comparison is
  between two processes, which share only the wall clock. "stalled alert raised", once on 16 November

- **"study runner reported running while trials log elsewhere"** (`tests/test_review_fixes.py`), once,
  on 17 November, in the full run of the repair ("Tests" below): one status call six seconds after a

### The repair of the loop

As it stands after both commits (`cb7ee1b`, `053cd8c`):

- While a session or a training run is in flight, the loop asks its own count of the time used four
  times a second and ends the session or the run when the count has reached the limit. It hands to
  `check()` that the limit was the bound: the campaign then stops for the limit, whatever a second
  count says. A second count can say "not yet" for two reasons: the count is rounded to 0.1 s when the
  state is saved in between, and a wall clock that was ahead may have been set back.
- The time used is the larger of two counts since the last save, the wall clock's and the monotonic
  clock's; `nnremote.py` has counted a job's time so since 15 November. A wall clock that is set back
  cannot put the limit off, and time that the monotonic clock may leave out (a machine asleep) still
  counts, as it did, for a session and a run in flight too.
- The bound of a session that hangs (`agent_timeout_s`) and the wait for a run that does not end are
  measured on the monotonic clock (before: on the wall clock).
- A limit, named in a `shortcut:` comment: a wall clock that is stepped forward and back again adds the
  step forward at each save that meets it, and a look at a session or a run in flight that meets it
  finds the limit reached when less than the step is left of it. So in that WSL a campaign can also end
  early by up to nine seconds for each such save or look, on top of the 9 %, and the stop's line can
  then name a count that is below the limit.
- Weighed and not taken: the monotonic clock alone, under which the time that a machine spends asleep
  would not count on Linux and macOS; and a count from the process's start, which would not add such
  steps and needs more state, for a gain of seconds on a machine whose clock is at fault.
- `references/loop.md` says in one sentence how the time is counted.

Every change in the behaviour of an existing feature, against the loop of `36a4857`:

- A campaign that the wall-clock limit ends during a session always stops with "limit reached: hours"
  and exit code 0, and runs the confirmation of a kept change (before: at times "the agent session
  hung", exit code 1 and no confirmation).
- A campaign that the wall-clock limit ends during a training run always stops for the limit (before:
  where the wall clock was set back between the loop's look and its second count, it stopped with
  "stop requested: the training run ... was stopped from outside the loop", with exit code 0 and
  without the confirmation). No machine has shown this; it is read from the code and shown by the new
  check.
- Where the wall clock is set back during a campaign, the limit comes when the monotonic clock says so
  (before: later by the step).
- Where the monotonic clock runs fast, the limit, the bound of a session that hangs and the wait for a
  run that does not end come early by as much (before: on time by the wall clock). In that WSL an
  `agent_timeout_s` of 900 s is about 818 s.
- A session that starts with less than a second left of the limit is ended when the limit is reached
  (before: one second after its start).
- A session in flight on a machine that is suspended for longer than `agent_timeout_s` is not ended as
  a hang on waking where the monotonic clock stops during the suspension, which PEP 418 says of Linux
  and macOS (before: it was, with "the agent session hung" and exit code 1). The wall-clock limit counts
  the suspension as before and ends the session if it is used up. The second reader pointed to this.

The guard is not touched.

### The independent reading of the repair

On my own initiative, before any push: a fresh agent on another model (Opus 5.5), with read access only
and no context of mine, briefed to check the two commits `cb7ee1b` and `463275d` for correctness. It ran
no test and was not stopped by a safeguard. Its points, most serious first, each with my answer:

1. **A session in flight was no longer cut off by the wall clock where that clock is ahead, as after
   a machine's sleep** (it called this likely; of medium weight). `cb7ee1b` worked out a session's
   bound when the session began and timed it on the monotonic clock alone. With ten minutes left of
   the limit and a machine that sleeps for an hour one minute in, the loop of `36a4857` ended the
   session within a quarter of a second of waking; that of `cb7ee1b` would have let it run nine minutes
   more. True, and a regression of mine for one commit, which was never pushed. Fixed in `053cd8c`:
   the bound is gone, and the loop asks its count, which has both clocks, at each look.
2. **The reference page said more than the code did** (certain; low). "Where the two clocks differ the
   campaign ends by the one that is ahead" was not so for a session in flight, and the larger count is
   taken from one save to the next, so the total can exceed what either clock counted in all. Fixed:
   the sentence now says "from one save of the state to the next" and "no later than by the one that
   is ahead", and the comment in the code says the same.
3. **A step forward of the wall clock at the wrong moment can end a campaign a few seconds early, with
   a count below the limit in the stop's line** (likely; low; partly by design). True in that WSL.
   Accepted as the limit that the `shortcut:` comment names, which now names this path too.
4. **The bound of a hang and the wait for a run that does not end now follow a clock that runs 10 %
   fast in that WSL** (certain; low). True. Accepted, and listed among the changes above.
5. **The new check is sound, and narrow** (likely; low): both of its cases fail on the old loop and
   pass on the new, but it is tied to exact numbers, and it had no case of a wall clock that runs
   ahead. Answered with two more cases: a machine that sleeps during a session, and a run in flight.
   The numbers stay: the clocks are the test's own, so they are the same on every machine. A hang with
   no limit near is what the older check "a session that hangs is ended after agent_timeout_s" asks.
6. **Not a regression, but still there** (unsure, by reading): a training run that the limit ends is
   reported as stopped from outside the loop where the wall clock is set back between the loop's look
   and its second count. True, and not only for that WSL: a clock that is corrected after a machine
   wakes does the same. I had weighed handing the bound to `check()` there too and had left it. Fixed
   in `053cd8c`, with the first check that this path has had.

It checked and found sound: that no time is counted twice between a save and the count; that the two
marks are always set together; resuming, a detached start and the replacement of the state; the exit
codes; the GPU time of a run; and that the change to the tests' stand-in alters no check's question.

**The reading of the answer.** Because the first form had a gap, the change that became `053cd8c` was
read before its commit by a second fresh agent of the same kind (Opus 5.5, read access only, no
context of mine, a brief on correctness; it ran nothing and was not stopped by a safeguard). It found
nothing wrong. It traced a session and a run by hand for the limit reached in flight, a hang with the
limit far off, a stop request, a stop for paid usage, no wall-clock limit, the confirmation and a run
that does not end: each gives the intended reason and exit code, saves the state once and counts no
time twice. It traced the check's four cases against this loop and against that of `cb7ee1b` and got
the values that the runs gave (under "Tests"). It named three things that are not defects, all listed
above: the early end in that WSL, the second that a session no longer gets past the limit, and the
hang's bound across a machine's suspension. It did not read the stand-in agent of the tests or the two
helpers that end a session's processes and look for paid usage.

From documentation only: which monotonic clocks count the time a machine is suspended. PEP 418's table
of clocks, read on 17 November 2026: Linux's `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` and macOS's `mach_absolute_time` do not,
Windows's `GetTickCount64` does, and Windows's `QueryPerformanceCounter` has a question mark there. No
machine was put to sleep. The count does not depend on the answer, since the larger of the two holds.

### The ledger

`docs/upgrade/LEDGER.md` has 1,703 rows now (1,699 before). The four new rows are in the note `round8`.
One is adopted and built: the loop counts its time on two clocks and names the bound that ended a
session. Three are rejected, each with the reason: the monotonic clock alone, under which a machine's
time asleep would not count; a count from the process's start; and run deadlines and heartbeat ages on
a clock that cannot be stepped. The decisions: Adopt 529 (386 finished, 143 unfinished), Trial 237,

### What the other readers found

- **The second reader** confirmed the first three changes by reading and with random texts, and found
  the fourth wrong in one case: where a command substitution reaches across an escaped quote

  whether a stretch between two escaped quotes opens a `$( )`, backticks or a `${ }` that it does not
  close, and such a text keeps the spelling of 17 November. It also named twelve branches without a
  row; each has a row now, with a harmless twin.
- **The third reader** found no claim that fails. It named limits of `reaches()` that its comment did
  not: an escaped `\$(` counts as one that opens, and so does a `${` in quotes inside a `$( )`. Both
  keep the older spelling where the newer would do, which costs time and no question. It named one
  case that the comment now states (the word of a default, `${X:-\"d\"}`, stands in the name's place
  before the text is judged), four branches without a check, which have one now, and four sentences
  of the reference that said less than the code. The code did not change for it.
- **The fourth reader** found no claim that fails: it compared every call of the new lookup with the
  old one on 627 generated lines (`cd`, `pushd`, subshells, `git -C`, here-documents, PowerShell's
  `Set-Location`): 44,026 calls, no result and no answer differs. Three things were done on its
  report. The comment said "per call" where one run of the hook may check several files of a patch;
  it says "per run of the hook" now. A lookup that failed was kept for the run; it is made again now,
  as before, so that nothing changes where a server answers the second time. And the check takes
  four of the five branches it named: a path object, a full name, a `~` word and a failed lookup. The
  fifth, several calls in one run of the hook, has no check of its own: they share the kept lookups,
  which is right as long as the guard writes nothing between them, and it writes only its audit log,
  after the checks. Two smaller points are answered and not changed: a full name is kept once for
  each working folder, which costs a lookup and no answer, and the table has no limit, since it lasts
  one run of the hook.

### What I found while fixing

- **The second kind of line that passed**: `cat <<'EOF'`, a line `don't print("a \" b")`, `EOF`, and
  then `echo "x > eval/metrics.py" 'y'`. The reading of 16 November, the document with the quotes
  that pair in it, asked about it; `63bfdf6` put the document without any of its quotes in that
  reading's place. Both are made now.
- **The second slow line, by timing.** The spelling of 17 November makes a piece of every escaped
  quote, and the guard looks up every run of touching pieces on disk as a path. `curl -s -d` with a
  compact JSON body of 100 fields (1,425 characters, 400 escaped quotes) took 21.7 seconds on Windows,
  50 fields 8.8 seconds, and 0.08 seconds before 17 November. **My first estimate of that cost, made
  without measuring, was too low by a factor of about 35.** The text is now cut at each `\"`, and the
  stretches without a backslash, a `$`, a backtick or an apostrophe go, with the quotes between them,
  into one piece in apostrophes (`'a " b'`); a stretch with one of those stays in `"..."` as it came.
- **A change that proved unnecessary**: an early end, at a blank, of the chains of pieces that are
  looked up. It made no measurable difference once the spelling had the fewest pieces, and it is taken
  out again, so that function is as on the public `main`.
- **The answer that went from refused to allowed** (point 3): where a quoted text leaves a
  substitution open, the guard pairs the quotes of the texts behind it anew, so their spelling decides
  what it takes for commands there. Therefore the rule for the rest of the command: from the first
  text on that a substitution reaches out of, across an escaped quote or past the text's end
  (`"$(dirname "$0")"`), every `"..."` keeps the spelling of 17 November. From there on each reading
  is the text which that day's guard made, and in front of it every text is a whole piece. What a
  substitution runs is read from the line as it came, as in every version.
- **The third slow line, by timing, and a wrong sentence of mine.** I had written that making the
  older readings too is what costs time on a long here-document. Timing the public `main` showed
  that the cost is its own: each reading is one more pass of every rule over the line, and each pass
  looked every word up on disk again, on Windows about 0.13 ms for a file that is not there. For the
  script of 1,500 lines that is 138,475 lookups for 3,877 different words. Where the older reading
  differs from the newer ones my first change did add passes: a document of 88 KB took 15 seconds
  against 10 on the public `main`. The guard now keeps what a lookup found, by working folder and
  word, for the run of the hook: 8 seconds for the script and 4 for that document.

### Every change in what the guard asks, refuses or allows

Against the public `main` (`5dcd2ec`), each with its reason and its test:

- **Asked about again**: the two kinds of line of point 1. Reason: the older readings stay. Test: four
  rows.
- **Asked about, where the public `main` refuses**: a sealed file named between escaped quotes in a
  text that the guard does not read as a command of its own, as in `ssh host "cat \"<sealed file>\""`.
  Reason: the refusal came from a path that the guard made of the name and the quote behind it, an
  effect of the spelling of 17 November; with the fewest pieces that path is not made. Every version
  before 17 November asked, and the public `main` asks about the same word written in apostrophes
  (seven pairs put to it). Where nobody can answer, a question is a refusal, so nothing passes there.
  Test: rows for a sealed file that a text only names (asked about), for code that reads one in
  `python -c` and in `sh -c`, and for a file in the sealed folder (refused).
- **Refused as before**: text handed to a shell or an interpreter on this machine. `sh -c`, `bash -c`,
  `eval`, `python -c` and `node -e` with a sealed file between escaped quotes are refused by every
  version put to them, back to the one before round 8. Behind a text that a substitution reaches out
  of, the refusal of the public `main` stays as it is.
- **Answered for what they hold, where the public `main` gives the timer's question**: the three kinds
  of long line of point 2. Test: two time checks (the 120 KB line; a JSON body of 2,000 fields) and a
  check that counts the lookups of a word. By the code and not measured: so may a call be that names
  a file on a place which answers slowly, such as a network share, since each word is waited for once
  and not by every rule and reading. A lookup that fails is made again as before.
- **No answer to a read-only subagent differs** on the generated lines. On the probe lines the two
  kinds of point 1 are refused to it again.
- **Not changed**: what the guard asks or refuses for the line as it came; the routine mark; the
  audit log.

### What it costs, and the limits that stay

- **The slow case of point 5**: `cd "$(dirname "$0")" && curl -d` with the 100 fields. The code names
  it as a shortcut with what would lift it: keeping the spelling of 17 November only up to where the
  reaching substitution ends, which takes finding that end where the guard's pairs and the shell's
  part ways. The ledger holds it as adopted and unfinished.
- **Each reading is a pass.** Six long lines of 4.5 to 71 KB (500 and 4,000 texts with an escaped
  quote, documents of 500 and 4,000 lines, `curl` bodies of 500 and 4,000 escaped fields) take 0.2
  to 2.2 seconds here, 0.4 to 7.4 seconds and once the timer's question on the public `main`, and 0.1
  to 1.4 seconds on the guard of 16 November. The script of 1,500 lines takes 7.7 seconds on the
  guard before round 8 (two readings), 10.0 on that of 16 November (three), 23.1 on the public `main`
  (seven) and 8.0 here (seven).
- **`reaches()` counts** backticks and `${` instead of following them. The count leans to the kept
  spelling, which costs time and no question; on 6,000 generated lines with such pieces in every
  order no answer differed from the public `main`'s other than the kind of point 4.
- **Unchanged limits**: text handed to `cmd /c`; the timer cannot answer during one search of a
  pattern; PowerShell's `""` and `''` escapes and curly quotes were not tested in depth.
